## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{20}{100}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why does an admitted plan still need permission on every control tick?_

A trajectory can be feasible when it arrives and become unsafe while the machine follows it. The body lags its reference, a payload or a hot motor erodes braking authority, a person steps into the path, or the learned proposer stalls with its last command still in force. A machine that checks only before motion begins discovers these changes after the energy is already moving, and the proposer cannot be trusted to notice them, because nothing in its output bounds stopping distance, actuator effort, or timing. Learned proposals therefore need an independent permission path that re-checks current conditions on every tick, keeps useful motion inside a stopping envelope, corrects a command when a feasible correction exists, and holds a response it can execute without the proposer before the remaining margin is spent. Each of those guarantees depends on bounded sensing error, available actuator force, and a decision delivered on time. Enforcement joins these conditions at the causal boundary, where a permitted command becomes motion that software cannot undo.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain the relationship between tracking accuracy, command permission, and independent enforcement at the actuator boundary
- Calculate the finished stopping budget and the speed ceiling it sets from response delay, braking, localization, and tracking error
- Derive how momentum and commanded effort change the remaining safety margin, and the contact force at a latch and at a handover that caps approach speed
- Explain how a control barrier function limits motion while its model, sensing, actuator, and timing assumptions hold
- Formulate a quadratic program that minimally adjusts a proposal within feasible actuator and safety constraints
- Select state-matched fallback responses when sensing, computation, or actuator limits invalidate normal enforcement
- Distinguish the permission path's unrated performance checks from the certified drive, scanner, and arm safety functions that carry the protective claim beneath it
- Construct an enforcement record and formulate the admitted command that binds each check to its detector, its fallback response, and the records it consumes

:::
## Deterministic Safety Filters and Permission Gating {#sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper}

Every physical AI system ends in the same act. A command leaves software, becomes current in a motor winding, and puts momentum into a world that does not roll back. Safety enforcement is the runtime mechanism that decides, one control tick at a time, whether the next command may cross that causal boundary. Checking a plan once before it runs does not settle the question, because admission judges the plan against the state the planner predicted, and the machine then executes it against the state it actually reaches. Between those two moments the body can lag its reference, an actuator can run short of torque, a person can step into the aisle, and the learned proposer can stall or emit a setpoint the plan never contained. Enforcement exists so that none of these events is discovered only after the energy has been delivered.

The central constraint is that the learned proposer can neither be trusted with that decision nor be discarded. Its competence is what makes the machine useful, yet nothing in its output bounds stopping distance, actuator effort, or timing. Enforcement resolves the tension by separating proposal from permission (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}) and giving the permission side three jobs. It must hold a stopping reservation, the clearance the machine needs to arrest its motion from the current state; it must correct a proposal minimally when a feasible correction exists; and it must select a response it can execute without the proposer when none does. We develop these in that order. The tracking bound and the stopping budget fix the reservation and the speed it allows. Actuator authority and the control barrier function turn the reservation into a constraint on the next command. The least-change filter and its cycle budget make the correction timely. The fallback ladder, and the certified safety functions beneath it, supply the response that survives a failed check, and the enforcement record binds every check to its evidence.

On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the safety microcontroller (MCU) admits the run down the aisle only after the matched stop suffix named in its trajectory record (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract) is resident in the MCU's memory and feasible from its commitment entry state. Admission also requires an independently executable, state-matched fallback from every state reachable during the admitted motion before commitment; the attached suffix need not fit those earlier states. That admission checks the plan once, before the motion starts. The machine then executes it one millisecond tick at a time, and enforcement is the check made on every one of those ticks, together with the response it selects when even the resident stop no longer fits.

An invalid command must be intercepted before it reaches the drive, because once current in a winding imparts momentum, an exception handler cannot recall it (@sec-boundary-bedrock-laws). Enforcement therefore keeps the task competence of learned policies while denying them authority over geometric clearance, thermal limits, and human-safety invariants. The enforcer\index{Enforcer} of @sec-nervous-cadences, the permission path's per-tick gatekeeper, sits on the permission side of the proposal boundary. It is a hard real-time component that evaluates candidate proposals, verifies invariant state bounds, and holds the exclusive hardware authority to permit current flow or command a fallback stop.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_pa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan-to-Act gating edge."}
*Enforcement sits on the Plan-to-Act edge: no proposal reaches a drive unchecked.*
:::

In the architecture this chapter follows, the enforcer executes on a dedicated microcontroller wired to the sensing and drive interfaces it needs. It checks each candidate command before the drive can apply it. A packet firewall offers a limited software analogy: a sender may request an operation without having authority to perform it. Unlike a packet filter, the enforcer must also account for momentum already present in the plant and preserve an achievable response when it refuses a request.

The architecture separates a capable proposer, a resident protective controller, and an output selector. This is the **Simplex architecture**\index{Simplex architecture!dual-controller model}[^fn-simplex-online-upgrade] [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using]: the proposer supplies useful candidates, while the permission path retains the exclusive ability to select a physically feasible response without waiting for it. The hardware allocation that makes this separation effective is developed in @sec-placement. The first quantity the enforcer needs is how far the body can stray from the reference it is asked to follow, because every clearance the permission path defends must also contain that error.

[^fn-simplex-online-upgrade]: **Simplex Architecture**: The design came from Carnegie Mellon in the 1990s as a way to upgrade the controller of a running plant without stopping it. An untested new controller drove the plant while a simple verified controller and a switching rule stood ready to take it back [@seto1998simplex]. The learned proposer occupies the untested controller's seat, and the design's premise, that the region from which the verified controller can still recover is known in advance, is the stopping envelope this chapter computes. \index{Simplex architecture!online upgrade}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-lease-stop
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TIMING CONTRACT AND THE LEASE-EXPIRY WORST CASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the lease paragraph below; the cycle timeline, @tbl-12-fallback-hierarchy,
# │          the enforcement record, and the summary reuse these strings.
# │ Goal:    state the three timers and the delay from last renewal to brake onset.
# │ Show:    chunk rate, lease, heartbeat rate and timeout, self-watchdog,
# │          tick, bus cycle, brake onset, renewal-to-onset delay; the
# │          evidence-age refusal threshold (budgeted observation age plus the
# │          clock-conversion bound) read by cycle stage 2 and the record. The
# │          base stall is priced in calc-enforcement-stopping-budget, after the
# │          spare is set.
# │ How:     the same RM/AISLE fields that size the lease in @sec-nervous-cadences.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementLeaseStop:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    heartbeat_rate = AISLE.heartbeat_rate  # category: chosen
    heartbeat_timeout = AISLE.heartbeat_timeout  # category: chosen
    self_watchdog = AISLE.mcu_self_watchdog  # category: chosen
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (observation age the budget charges, row 5)
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (clock-conversion bound, @sec-perception-observation-contract)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    renewal_to_onset = (lease + tick + bus + onset).to(millisecond)
    age_threshold = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # dispatch-age qualification threshold

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(chunk_period < lease, "One chunk period must fit inside the lease.")
    check(heartbeat_timeout < lease, "A total host stall must trip the heartbeat before the lease expires.")
    check(abs(lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "The chunk lease is 60 ms.")
    check(abs(renewal_to_onset.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "Brake onset comes 82 ms after the last valid renewal.")
    check(abs(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, "The budgeted observation age is 51.6 ms.")
    check(abs(age_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, "The dispatch-age qualification threshold is 51.8 ms.")
    # fig12_canonical_fallback_ladder.svg and parts/images/svg/fig_part3_record_chain.svg draw 1 kHz, 60 ms, and 51.6 ms from these guards.
    check(abs(tick.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "The hand-drawn figures label the MCU tick 1 kHz.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate_hz_str = fmt(chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    lease_ms_str = fmt_latency(lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    heartbeat_rate_hz_str = fmt(heartbeat_rate.to(hertz).magnitude, precision=0)
    heartbeat_timeout_ms_str = fmt_latency(heartbeat_timeout, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    self_watchdog_ms_str = fmt_latency(self_watchdog, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tick_ms_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tick_us_str = fmt_latency(tick, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    loop_rate_str = fmt_frequency((1 / tick).to(hertz))
    bus_ms_str = fmt_latency(bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    onset_ms_str = fmt_latency(onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_to_onset_ms_str = fmt_latency(renewal_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_threshold_str = fmt_latency(age_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```
## The Tracker Handoff and Dynamic Reference Envelopes {#sec-enforcement-handoff}

Even when communication latency is zero and the safety filter admits every reference command without delay, physical robots follow reference trajectories imperfectly. Mechanical compliance, inertia, and non-ideal motor dynamics inevitably produce tracking discrepancies. The feedback tracker—the closed-loop controller responsible for translating admitted references into actuator effort (@sec-planning-handoff)—must rigorously bound this deviation across the entire maneuver. We formalize this deviation using a **worst-case tracking error tube** ($\epsilon_{\text{track}}$), which defines an upper bound on the spatial departure of the tracked position output from its nominal reference. In our tracking formulations, $\mathbf{x}(t)$ and $\mathbf{r}(t)$ denote the actual and reference positions evaluated in identical spatial coordinates, rather than a full state vector conflating position, velocity, and internal joint angles. For whole-body systems such as mobile manipulators, the execution stack defines a declared output map or metric weighting that bounds the maximum physical swept-volume displacement in meters. The safety enforcer depends directly on this bound: any spatial clearance reserved around a planned reference path must guarantee physical containment of the actual robot body.

Provided that the physical system begins within an initial qualified error region and operating parameters—such as reference velocity, command acceleration, payload mass, external disturbances, and actuator temperature—stay within their validated operating envelope, the feedback controller guarantees the transient position-error bound:
$$\|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{r}(t)\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}} \quad \forall t \ge 0.$$
This guarantee forms a software contract between the tracking layer and the safety enforcer\index{Enforcer!tracking contract}. Rather than re-analyzing raw plant dynamics or reconstructing low-level controller state on every millisecond control cycle, the enforcer consumes this certified error bound as an invariant. However, this contract confines physical motion to the $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$\index{Tracking error bound} tube only while the operational conditions used to establish the certificate remain valid.

The magnitude of $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ is a physical distance dictated by hardware properties: reflected rotor inertia ($N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$, @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia), gearbox backlash, structural compliance, and actuator torque saturation\index{Actuator torque limits}. While a steady-state stiffness calculation balances constant external disturbances against closed-loop restoring force\index{Closed-loop stiffness}, steady-state metrics fail to capture transient overshoot, phase lag, or settling oscillations excited during aggressive maneuvers. Consequently, engineering teams cannot rely on static linear approximations; they must establish the tracking tube bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ through full-envelope dynamic qualification testing across worst-case operational maneuvers.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-tracking-bound
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE BASE'S TRACKING BOUND
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the tracking-bound paragraphs immediately below.
# │ Goal:    state the inset the enforcer applies and what a doubled error costs.
# │ Show:    the base's tracking bound and the error if wear doubled it.
# │ How:     AISLE.eps_track, the same field row 7 of the stopping budget uses.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementTrackingBound:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_doubled = (2 * eps_track).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "The base's tracking bound is 40 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_track_str = fmt_length(eps_track, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_doubled_str = fmt_length(eps_doubled, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

For our baseline warehouse mobile manipulator, the certified dynamic qualification target is $\epsilon_{\text{track}} =$ `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` (illustrative; see the Reader Guide). The tracking controller sustains this bound only while three coupled operational constraints remain satisfied: reference trajectories must not demand accelerations exceeding drive torque limits, external disturbance forces must remain below $d_{\text{max}}$, and actuator coils must operate below their continuous thermal derating thresholds (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles\index{Joule heating}) and DC bus voltage limits. A reference trajectory demanding acceleration beyond peak torque drives the actuators into saturation\index{Actuator saturation}, causing the physical chassis to lag behind the command. Without aggressive anti-windup clamping, the integrator state accumulates severe windup\index{Integrator windup}, prolonging recovery long after the reference demand subsides. Outside this qualified operating envelope, the tracking certificate is void, and the system loses its guaranteed error bound.

Because the physical robot can deviate from its planned reference by up to $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ in any direction, the safety architecture must subtract this uncertainty margin directly from the admissible workspace. Let $h$ measure the spatial clearance remaining around a reference. To guarantee that the physical robot maintains non-negative clearance, the enforcer applies an inset contraction:
$$h_{\text{contracted}}(\mathbf{r}) = h(\mathbf{r}) - \epsilon_{\text{track}} \ge 0.$$
A reference trajectory that maintains nominal clearance $c$ from a warehouse rack upright guarantees the physical chassis only $c - \epsilon_{\text{track}}$ of actual clearance. Consequently, the safety enforcer evaluates reference commands against a contracted boundary that adds `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` to the nominal buffer. As detailed in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes, this tracking inset compounds directly with stopping distance budgets, where localization uncertainty and transport delay consume additional clearance. Mechanical wear poses an insidious operational risk here: if worn drive bearings, tire degradation, or altered motor parameters double the true tracking error to `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_doubled_str` without updating the enforcer's parameter registry, the physical base consumes an unbudgeted `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str` of clearance that the enforcer assumes remains available. An unmodeled tracking degradation silently undermines every higher-level safety margin.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Spatial clearance insetting from sensor covariance and transport delay originates in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
:::

To maintain safety guarantees in production, the runtime monitoring stack must treat $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ as an actively verified contract rather than a static design assumption. The underlying real-time middleware publishes $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ alongside its validity envelope, while hardware monitors compute the instantaneous tracking error $e(t) = \|\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{r}(t)\|$ on every 1 ms controller tick. If an unmodeled disturbance spike, wheel slippage on a slick surface, or actuator thermal throttling causes $e(t)$ to exceed $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, the tracking contract is broken. Upon detecting this violation, the safety enforcer revokes the admitted command and activates a state-matched emergency fallback maneuver. Maintaining physical containment during this transition requires that the fallback braking trajectory remains dynamically feasible even after the tracking bound is lost.

::: {#psp-enforcement-inset-margin .callout-perspective title="The inset margin invariant"}
A spatial stopping boundary must reserve margin for the tracking loop's qualified error bound. The runtime stopping envelope (@eq-enforce-stopping-envelope) incorporates this geometric inset alongside displacement accumulated during transport lag\index{Transport lag} before admitting reference trajectories. When safety barrier certificates\index{Barrier certificates} are formulated in non-spatial coordinates (such as energy or momentum limits), the safety layer must map the tracking tube into a corresponding conservative bound on barrier variation, rather than subtracting a scalar distance. Evaluating barrier certificates against nominal trajectory geometry alone risks admitting references whose physical tracking tubes intersect obstacle boundaries.
:::

Control theory provides rich methodologies for synthesizing tracking controllers, state observers, and disturbance rejection algorithms [@slotine1991applied; @astrom2021feedback]. In embedded industrial robotics, systems frequently deploy a **cascaded control hierarchy**\index{Cascaded control!tracking architecture}, where outer position loops feed intermediate velocity setpoints down to high-rate current loops. Alternatively, a **tracking Model Predictive Controller (MPC)**\index{Model Predictive Control!tracking layer} solves an online optimization problem over a receding horizon to generate optimal corrective control actions while respecting actuator bounds. From the perspective of the safety enforcer, the specific internal architecture of the tracking controller is abstracted away; the safety filter requires only that the chosen implementation certifies and guarantees a concrete tracking bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ under specified operational conditions.

Crucially, a tracking controller guarantees convergence to the reference path, not collision avoidance. A well-tuned tracker will follow an erroneous trajectory directly into a warehouse support column with high precision. Control Lyapunov functions[^fn-clf-tracking-convergence] mathematically formalize this asymptotic convergence toward reference targets; @sec-appendix-control-lyapunov details their theoretical foundation and demonstrates how optimization pipelines unify stabilizing Lyapunov objectives with forward-invariant safety barrier certificates.

[^fn-clf-tracking-convergence]: **Control Lyapunov Function**: A Lyapunov function certifies that an unforced system settles; a control Lyapunov function asks only that, at each state, some admissible input make it decrease. @artstein1983stabilization tied the existence of such a function to stabilizability by feedback, and @sontag1989universal gave an explicit formula that builds the stabilizing input from it. The barrier is its mirror image, keeping the state out of a region instead of pulling it toward a point, and when the two conflict the combined optimization relaxes convergence so that the barrier holds. \index{Control Lyapunov function!barrier counterpart}

This division of responsibilities cleanly separates trajectory tracking from safety enforcement. The low-level tracking controller focuses on driving the physical plant toward reference states, while the safety enforcer determines whether those references can be executed without violating invariant boundaries. The tracking error bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ bridges these subsystems: it quantifies the spatial divergence between admitted commands and physical execution. Because environmental disturbances, unmodeled payload shifts, or thermal current derating can rapidly widen this error tube, safety architectures must continuously verify physical performance against contracted assumptions. The downstream stopping envelope accounts for this tracking tube alongside sensor latency, braking distance, and localization drift, ensuring that the physical robot remains safely buffered from surrounding hazards.
## Stopping Envelopes {#sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes}

Every physical subsystem contributes an essential stopping term to the mobile manipulator's spatial budget at the warehouse rack end, with the base tracking error providing the final physical margin. One critical timing interval—the delay from proposal dispatch to runtime admission—is omitted from this spatial sum; the budget instead charges it against the temporal allowance preserved by the remaining clearance. The stopping envelope defines the set of physical states from which a validated braking maneuver can bring the machine to a complete rest before contacting an obstacle boundary. The underlying irreversibility principle (\ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}) establishes the governing test: $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$, with every constituent term bounded by qualified physical limits and empirical evidence. Our running calculation incorporates representative engineering limits, though physical deployment requires empirical qualification on the actual hardware platform. Guaranteeing this stopping capability directly constrains achievable vehicle speed, because velocity inflates communication and reaction latency linearly while inflating braking distance quadratically. At runtime, the enforcer must ensure the robot remains strictly within this safe envelope before any fault or unmodeled disturbance can manifest.

The pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ established in the stopping distance formulation of @sec-body-kinetic-momentum already accounts for the enforcer's permission evaluation cycle, budgeted alongside the lease communication path in @sec-nervous-cadences. The final remaining discrepancy is the physical tracking error between the commanded reference trajectory and the actual robot plant.

The safety enforcement layer accounts for this deviation using the tracking bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ established in @sec-enforcement-handoff, effectively offsetting the baseline stopping distance of @eq-body-stopping-distance. The enforcer can admit a candidate reference trajectory only if the plant—which may lag behind that reference by up to $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$—can still brake to a standstill within the available free distance $D_{\text{clear}}$. Combining physical clearance, latency, and velocity yields the composite admission test:
$$v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} + d_{\text{suffix}}(v) + \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} + \epsilon_{\text{track}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$$ {#eq-enforce-stopping-envelope}
Here, $d_{\text{suffix}}(v)$ represents the physical distance traversed during the braking maneuver from an initial speed $v$. For idealized constant-deceleration braking, this term simplifies to $v^2 / (2a_{\text{brake}})$. Under the realistic jerk-limited trajectory profiles analyzed in @sec-planning-behavior-seam, $d_{\text{suffix}}(v)$ is governed by @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix, which incorporates the additional displacement accrued during finite jerk transitions. The term $\delta_{\text{loc}}$ denotes the localization uncertainty bound, while $\delta_{\text{margin}}$ provides an explicit protective safety cushion. The left-hand side sums the baseline stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}(v)$ from @eq-body-stopping-distance with the tracking inset $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, completing the physical derivation presented in @sec-appendix-systems-stopping.

This inequality defines a viable conditional stopping region in state space. Within this set, the combined reaction latency and braking profile fit within the measured obstacle clearance. Operating outside this boundary violates the stopping reservation under the qualified model assumptions, though conservative engineering margins do not imply that an instantaneous collision is certain under all conceivable emergency maneuvers. Crucially, per-tick enforcement must maintain this stopping reservation over the entire control epoch until the next validated command can take effect, rather than merely verifying instantaneous feasibility at the sample instant.

Whenever a proposed trajectory requires a stopping distance in @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope that exceeds the measured clearance along the current heading, the enforcer rejects the command. Because the robot moves directionally, the stopping envelope is fundamentally anisotropic\index{Stopping envelope!Anisotropy}. Heading dictates which obstacles threaten forward travel and consume braking clearance, while localization uncertainty and the robot's swept geometric volume demand clearance margins around the entire perimeter.

### Sizing the composite stopping budget {#sec-enforcement-composite-budget}

The composite stopping budget integrates these disparate physical claims into the **spatial footprint of the chunk lease**, the bounded execution window formalized in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing under which an admitted action executes. This budget reserves clearance for sensor transduction lag, compute scheduling delays, physical actuator engagement, trajectory deceleration profiles, and mechanical tracking divergence. To ensure mathematical and operational validity, every constituent term must be evaluated under identical, worst-case operating conditions; otherwise, their linear combination cannot provide an authoritative admission guarantee.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-stopping-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE FINISHED STOPPING BUDGET OF THE WAREHOUSE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: row 7 and aisle-speed prose below, @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget.
# │ Goal:    add the tracking inset (row 7), then choose the aisle speed that the
# │          finished budget allows.
# │ Show:    each row's term, value, running total, and remainder at the drive
# │          limit; the same terms at the aisle speed; the ceiling; the time rows;
# │          the missed-tick cost reused by the cycle list; the walking-person
# │          ceiling (moved from @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion); the
# │          base stall at the aisle speed (distance added, overrun past D_clear);
# │          the Delta_da allocation charged against the timing allowance and
# │          the reserve it leaves.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE fields; jerk bound = peak jerk of the reference C2
# │          polynomial at the drive limit (calc_c2_stop_suffix);
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance / _time (row 6, stop rows);
# │          calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity (ceilings, solved numerically);
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with tau + a/(2j) (closed-form
# │          cross-check above a^2/j); RM.intent_inference_latency, the
# │          computed prefill-plus-decode latency (time row).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_c2_stop_suffix,
    calc_scurve_stop_distance,
    calc_scurve_stop_time,
    calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity,
    calc_max_permitted_velocity,
    calc_safe_stopping_distance,
    calc_free_space_expiry,
)
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_acceleration, fmt_jerk, fmt_magnitude, fmt_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementStoppingBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible, loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (excludes Delta_da)
    delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission.to(
        millisecond
    )  # category: illustrative (allocation of @sec-placement-isolation-decisions, not yet measured)
    v_human = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 K)
    mu_inspected = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (deployed INT4 prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)
    t_stall = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (proposer stall before any brake)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_path = (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus).to(millisecond)
    overhead = (delta_loc + delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    # Jerk bound: the peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial at the drive limit (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    v_plateau = (a_brake**2 / j_brake).to(meter / second)
    ramp_delay = (a_brake / (2 * j_brake)).to(millisecond)
    c2_drive = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_drive, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    c2_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)

    # Rows 1-7 at the drive limit, in book order
    brake_drive = (v_drive**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    onset_drive = (v_drive * t_act).to(millimeter)
    lease_drive = (v_drive * lease_path).to(millimeter)
    age_drive = (v_drive * t_age).to(millimeter)
    shape_drive = (c2_drive - brake_drive).to(millimeter)
    inset = eps_track.to(millimeter)
    run1 = brake_drive
    run2 = run1 + overhead
    run3 = run2 + onset_drive
    run4 = run3 + lease_drive
    run5 = run4 + age_drive
    run6 = run5 + shape_drive
    run7 = run6 + inset
    left = [
        (d_clear - run1).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run2).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run3).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run4).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run5).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run6).to(millimeter),
        (d_clear - run7).to(millimeter),
    ]

    # The same terms at the aisle speed
    brake_aisle = (v_aisle**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    onset_aisle = (v_aisle * t_act).to(millimeter)
    lease_aisle = (v_aisle * lease_path).to(millimeter)
    age_aisle = (v_aisle * t_age).to(millimeter)
    shape_aisle = (c2_aisle - brake_aisle).to(millimeter)
    total_aisle = (brake_aisle + overhead + onset_aisle + lease_aisle + age_aisle + shape_aisle + inset).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - total_aisle).to(millimeter)
    # Base stall: a last proposal that keeps authority for the stall instead of
    # the lease adds the extra delay's travel to the finished budget.
    stall_added = (v_aisle * (t_stall - t_lease)).to(millimeter)
    stall_breach = (total_aisle + stall_added - d_clear).to(millimeter)

    # Speed is the one free term: the ceiling of @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope
    ceiling = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    # Above a^2/j the S-curve is constant braking at a_brake with the delay lengthened by a/(2j)
    ceiling_closed = calc_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay + ramp_delay, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    total_check = calc_safe_stopping_distance(
        v_drive, tau_delay + ramp_delay, a_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(millimeter)
    # Operands of @eq-enforce-speed-ceiling for the napkin-math notebook
    tau_eff = (tau_delay + ramp_delay).to(millisecond)
    d_avail = (d_clear - delta_loc - delta_margin - eps_track).to(millimeter)
    a_tau = (a_brake * tau_eff).to(meter / second)
    a_tau_sq = (a_tau**2).to(meter**2 / second**2)
    two_a_d = (2 * a_brake * d_avail).to(meter**2 / second**2)
    root_term = ((a_tau_sq + two_a_d) ** 0.5).to(meter / second)
    ceiling_hand = (root_term - a_tau).to(meter / second)

    # Time rows (no distance added)
    # Free-space expiry abreast of the occluded rack end (@eq-mem-free-space-expiry):
    # the free depth is the hull-to-rack side clearance.
    belief_life = calc_free_space_expiry(AISLE.side_clearance, delta_loc, delta_margin, v_human).to(millisecond)
    missed_tick = (v_aisle * t_tick).to(millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond)
    capture_to_admission_max = (t_age + t_latest).to(millisecond)
    capture_to_onset_max = (tau_delay + t_latest).to(millisecond)
    # Delta_da is not a term of tau_delay; the timing allowance pays for it.
    travel_da = (v_aisle * delta_da).to(millimeter)
    reserve_t = (t_latest - delta_da).to(millisecond)
    reserve_d = (spare - travel_da).to(millimeter)
    capture_to_onset = AISLE.t_capture_to_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # rows 1-3 of @tbl-04-event-ledger
    mu_min = (a_brake / ureg.standard_gravity).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_inspected = min(a_brake, (mu_inspected * ureg.standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2))
    # The floor caps the deceleration; the jerk bound belongs to the load and is unchanged.
    ceiling_inspected = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_inspected, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)

    # Walking person: v tau + d_stop(v) + v_h (tau + T_stop(v)) + overhead = d_clear.
    # The S-curve's distance and time are not one polynomial in v, so MLSysIM solves it numerically.
    overhead_all = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: derived (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track)
    v_walk = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track, approach_velocity=v_human
    ).to(meter / second)
    d_walk = (
        v_walk * tau_delay
        + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake)
        + v_human * (tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_time(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake))
        + overhead_all
    ).to(meter)
    # Why the walking-person ceiling is so low: below a^2/j the jerk-limited stop never
    # reaches a_brake and lasts 2 sqrt(v/j), far longer than v/a, and the person walks
    # for the whole stop.
    t_stop_walk = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    t_stop_walk_const = (v_walk / a_brake).to(millisecond)
    brake_walk = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_walk, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    closure_walk = (v_human * t_stop_walk).to(millimeter)
    # A reference polynomial rescaled to stop from v_walk at the full a_brake would need this jerk
    jerk_rescaled_walk = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_walk, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    # The same walking-person budget under constant-deceleration braking (no jerk bound):
    # v^2/2a + (tau + v_h/a) v + v_h tau + overhead - d_clear = 0, positive root
    _qa = 1 / (2 * a_brake)
    _qb = tau_delay + v_human / a_brake
    _qc = v_human * tau_delay + overhead_all - d_clear
    v_walk_const = ((-_qb + (_qb**2 - 4 * _qa * _qc) ** 0.5) / (2 * _qa)).to(meter / second)
    # Latency sensitivity of the static ceiling: 10 ms more pre-brake delay
    ceiling_plus10 = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(
        d_clear, tau_delay + 10 * millisecond, a_brake, j_brake, loc_margin=delta_loc, physical_margin=delta_margin + eps_track
    ).to(meter / second)
    ceiling_drop_10ms = (ceiling - ceiling_plus10).to(millimeter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(run1.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-6, "Row 1 running total is 562.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run2.magnitude - 712.5) < 1e-6, "Row 2 running total is 712.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run3.magnitude - 742.5) < 1e-6, "Row 3 running total is 742.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run4.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, "Row 4 running total is 835.5 mm.")
    check(abs(run5.magnitude - 912.9) < 1e-6, "Row 5 running total is 912.9 mm.")
    check(abs(j_brake.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "The jerk bound is the reference polynomial's 7.11 m/s^3 peak.")
    check(v_aisle >= v_plateau and v_drive >= v_plateau, "Both budget speeds reach the deceleration bound (trapezoidal regime).")
    check(abs(run6.magnitude - 1123.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 6 running total is 1123.84 mm.")
    check(abs(run7.magnitude - 1163.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 7 running total is 1163.84 mm.")
    check(abs(total_check.magnitude - run7.magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row 7 total must equal @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope at the drive limit.")
    check(abs(left[6].magnitude + 63.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 7 runs 63.84 mm past the clear distance.")
    check(abs(lease_path.magnitude - 62.0) < 1e-9, "Lease path is 62 ms.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - 133.6) < 1e-9, "tau_delay is 133.6 ms.")
    check(abs(ceiling.magnitude - ceiling_closed.magnitude) < 1e-9, "Numerical ceiling must match the closed form above a^2/j.")
    check(ceiling >= v_plateau, "The ceiling lies in the trapezoidal regime.")
    check(abs(ceiling.magnitude - 1.4367) < 5e-5, "Ceiling is 1.44 m/s.")
    check(abs(ceiling_hand.magnitude - ceiling.magnitude) < 1e-9, "The notebook's hand arithmetic must reproduce the ceiling.")
    check(abs(d_avail.magnitude - 910.0) < 1e-9, "Clearance left after the fixed allowances is 910 mm.")
    check(v_aisle < ceiling, "The chosen aisle speed must sit under the ceiling.")
    check(abs(total_aisle.magnitude - 968.9925) < 1e-6, "Budget at 1.3 m/s is 968.99 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 1e-6, "Spare at 1.3 m/s is 131.01 mm.")
    check(abs(stall_added.magnitude - 182.0) < 1e-6, "A 200 ms stall adds 182 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(stall_added > spare, "The stall's added travel exceeds the whole spare.")
    check(abs(stall_breach.magnitude - 50.9925) < 5e-3, "The stall runs 51.0 mm past the clear distance.")
    # 2026-09-28 (M1/M2): the deployed intent model is INT4; its full computed inference replaces the FP16 weight sweep.
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(t_intent > t_lease, "The intent inference cannot renew a chunk lease.")
    check(belief_life.magnitude == 0.0, "Abreast of the occluded rack end the free-space claim expires at capture.")
    check(abs(missed_tick.magnitude - 1.3) < 1e-9, "One missed tick costs 1.3 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs(t_latest.magnitude - 100.775) < 5e-3, "The unallocated timing allowance is 100.8 ms at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(reserve_t.magnitude > 0 and reserve_d.magnitude > 0, "The Delta_da allocation must leave positive reserve.")
    check(abs((tau_delay + delta_da - capture_to_onset).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Capture to onset = tau_delay + Delta_da.")
    check(capture_to_onset < capture_to_onset_max, "The allocated capture-to-onset time must fall inside the latest onset.")
    check(
        abs((capture_to_onset_max - capture_to_admission_max - t_lease - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "Admission-to-onset must contain the lease, tick, bus, and drive onset exactly once.",
    )
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, "Friction premise is 0.204.")
    check(abs(ceiling_inspected.magnitude - 1.2309) < 5e-5, "Inspected-floor ceiling is 1.23 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_walk.magnitude - 0.2599) < 5e-5, f"Walking-person ceiling should be 0.260 m/s, got {v_walk}.")
    check(v_walk < v_plateau, "The walking-person stop never reaches the deceleration bound.")
    check(abs((d_walk - d_clear).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6, "At the walking-person ceiling the budget must fill the clear distance exactly.")
    check(abs(t_stop_walk.magnitude - 382.38) < 5e-2, "The jerk-limited stop from the walking-person ceiling lasts about 382 ms.")
    check(t_stop_walk > 2.9 * t_stop_walk_const, "Below a^2/j the jerk-limited stop lasts roughly three times a constant-deceleration stop.")
    check(closure_walk > 10 * brake_walk, "The person closes more than ten times the base's own braking travel.")
    check(jerk_rescaled_walk > 5 * j_brake, "Reaching a_brake from the walking-person ceiling would need several times the jerk bound.")
    check(abs(v_walk_const.magnitude - 0.6371) < 5e-4, "Without the jerk bound the walking-person ceiling would be 0.64 m/s.")
    check(ceiling_drop_10ms.magnitude > 0, "More pre-brake delay must lower the ceiling.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    ceiling_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling, precision=2)
    ceiling_inspected_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_inspected, precision=2)
    v_walk_str = fmt_velocity(v_walk, precision=2)
    v_plateau_str = fmt_velocity(v_plateau, precision=2)
    v_human_str = fmt_velocity(v_human, precision=1)
    t_stop_walk_str = fmt_latency(round(t_stop_walk.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_stop_walk_const_str = fmt_latency(round(t_stop_walk_const.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    brake_walk_str = fmt_length(round(brake_walk.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    closure_walk_str = fmt_length(round(closure_walk.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    jerk_rescaled_walk_str = fmt_jerk(round(jerk_rescaled_walk.magnitude) * meter / second**3, precision=0)
    v_walk_const_str = fmt_velocity(v_walk_const, precision=2)
    ceiling_drop_10ms_str = fmt_int(ceiling_drop_10ms.magnitude)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    j_brake_str = fmt_jerk(j_brake, precision=2)
    ramp_delay_str = fmt_latency(ramp_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_eff_str = fmt_latency(tau_eff, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    d_avail_str = fmt_length(d_avail, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_clear_mm_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    overhead_all_str = fmt_length(AISLE.fixed_overhead, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_margin_str = fmt_length(delta_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    a_tau_str = fmt(a_tau.magnitude, precision=4)
    a_tau_sq_str = fmt(a_tau_sq.magnitude, precision=4)
    two_a_d_str = fmt(two_a_d.magnitude, precision=2)
    root_term_str = fmt(root_term.magnitude, precision=4)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    lease_path_str = fmt_latency(lease_path, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    belief_life_str = fmt_latency(belief_life, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    missed_tick_str = fmt_length(missed_tick, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    capture_to_admission_max_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_admission_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    capture_to_onset_max_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_onset_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    delta_da_str = fmt_latency(delta_da, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    travel_da_str = fmt_length(travel_da, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    reserve_t_str = fmt_latency(reserve_t, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    reserve_d_str = fmt_length(reserve_d, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    capture_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(capture_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_inspected_str = fmt(mu_inspected, precision=2)
    inset_str = fmt_length(inset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    run6_str = fmt_length(run6, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    run7_str = fmt_length(run7, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    over7_str = fmt_length(-left[6], unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    total_aisle_str = fmt_length(total_aisle, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_stall_str = fmt_latency(t_stall, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    stall_added_str = fmt_length(stall_added, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    stall_breach_str = fmt_length(stall_breach, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    # Table cells (the column headers carry mm)
    brake_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(brake_drive, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    overhead_value_str = fmt_magnitude(overhead, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    onset_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(onset_drive, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    lease_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(lease_drive, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    age_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(age_drive, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    shape_drive_value_str = fmt_magnitude(shape_drive, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    inset_value_str = fmt_magnitude(inset, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    run1_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run1, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run2_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run2, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run3_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run3, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run4_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run4, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run5_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run5, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    run6_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run6, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    run7_value_str = fmt_magnitude(run7, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    left1_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[0], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left2_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[1], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left3_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[2], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left4_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[3], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left5_value_str = fmt_magnitude(left[4], millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    left6_math = fmt_math(fmt_magnitude(left[5], millimeter, precision=2, commas=True))
    left7_math = fmt_math(fmt_magnitude(left[6], millimeter, precision=2, commas=True))
    brake_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(brake_aisle, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    onset_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(onset_aisle, millimeter, precision=0, commas=True)
    lease_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(lease_aisle, millimeter, precision=1, commas=True)
    age_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(age_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    shape_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(shape_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    total_aisle_value_str = fmt_magnitude(total_aisle, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
    spare_value_str = fmt_magnitude(spare, millimeter, precision=2, commas=True)
```

With each constituent term quantified, we formalize the stopping envelope as the primary invariant enforced throughout runtime execution.

::: {#dfn-enforcement-stopping-envelope .callout-definition title="Stopping envelope"}

***Stopping envelope***\index{Stopping envelope!definition} is the set of plant states—parameterized by clearance and velocity along each degree of freedom—from which the resident emergency braking response, initiated after accounting for all worst-case delays, halts motion before reaching an obstacle boundary while preserving all localization, protective, and tracking margins.

1.  **Significance**: The envelope translates the abstract irreversibility requirement $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$ into an actionable runtime velocity ceiling. When approaching a rack end, the warehouse mobile manipulator's envelope restricts forward velocity to at most `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_str`, substantially below its mechanical drive limit of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str`.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a static geometric keep-out zone that depends solely on position, the stopping envelope is a dynamic construct governed by speed, system latencies, and braking authority. A given physical clearance safely admits a slow approach while strictly forbidding a high-speed transit.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the stopping envelope as a static, precomputed boundary. In practice, carried payload mass, surface traction coefficients, and motor thermal limits continuously reshape this boundary; calculating safety margins from ideal datasheet decelerations severely overestimates stopping authority when the machine is heavily loaded.

:::

For the warehouse mobile manipulator, the tracking bound of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.inset_str` provides the final physical distance margin incorporated into the budget. At the nominal `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit, incorporating the matched stop suffix of @sec-planning-behavior-seam pushes the cumulative stopping requirement to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.run6_str`, exceeding the available rack-end clearance of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str`. Factoring in the tracking inset expands this distance to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.run7_str`, producing a net overshoot of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.over7_str` beyond the physical boundary.

The terms comprising @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope unify the physical and computational constraints analyzed throughout this book: the credible deceleration and fixed allowances established by rigid-body mechanics (@sec-body-kinetic-momentum), the lease execution window derived from real-time scheduling cadences (@sec-nervous-cadences), the sensor observation age dictated by transduction latency (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration), the trajectory deceleration profile shaped by jerk limits (@sec-planning-behavior-seam), and the closed-loop tracking bound introduced here. The $C^2$ stop suffix replaces idealized constant deceleration ($v^2 / 2a_{\text{brake}}$) with jerk-limited S-curve deceleration governed by the peak jerk limit $j_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake_str`. Because both operating velocities reach the peak deceleration threshold, @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix models this maneuver by adding the displacement of half a jerk ramp:
$$d_{\text{suffix}}(v) = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} + v\,\frac{a_{\text{brake}}}{2 j_{\max}}.$$
Because this smoothly shaped trajectory consumes more physical clearance than discontinuous full-torque braking, we must determine the admissible transit velocity directly from the finished spatial budget.

Velocity remains the single operational variable the control architecture can dynamically modulate. Above the characteristic velocity threshold $a_{\text{brake}}^2/j_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_plateau_str`, the finite jerk ramps function equivalently to an added delay of $a_{\text{brake}}/(2j_{\max})$ prior to braking at constant deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$. Under these conditions, evaluating @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope at equality yields a quadratic equation in $v$, whose positive real root defines the authoritative **speed ceiling**\index{Speed ceiling!stopping envelope}:
$$v_{\max} = -a_{\text{brake}}\tau' + \sqrt{(a_{\text{brake}}\tau')^2 + 2a_{\text{brake}}D_{\text{avail}}}, \qquad \tau' = \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{a_{\text{brake}}}{2j_{\max}}, \qquad D_{\text{avail}} = D_{\text{clear}} - \delta_{\text{loc}} - \delta_{\text{margin}} - \epsilon_{\text{track}}$$ {#eq-enforce-speed-ceiling}
Below $a_{\text{brake}}^2/j_{\max}$, the deceleration trajectory never reaches the peak limit $a_{\text{brake}}$, rendering stopping distance non-quadratic in velocity; in this low-speed regime, MLSysIM evaluates @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope via numerical root-finding. The callout in \ref{nbk-enforcement-speed-ceiling} computes this ceiling for the mobile manipulator approaching the aisle rack end.

::: {#nbk-enforcement-speed-ceiling .callout-notebook title="The ceiling the budget sets"}

**Problem**: The warehouse mobile manipulator approaches the rack end with every stopping term of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget accounted except speed. What is the highest speed at which the jerk-limited stop still fits the clear distance, and how much clearance does a candidate aisle speed of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` leave?

**Variables**:

* $D_{\text{clear}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` (Illustrative; clear distance at the rack end).
* $\delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_loc_str` $+$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_margin_str` (Illustrative localization bound; chosen protective clearance), and $\epsilon_{\text{track}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.inset_str` (Illustrative; the qualification target of @sec-enforcement-handoff).
* $a_{\text{brake}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_brake_str` (Illustrative; credible loaded deceleration on a dry floor) and $j_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake_str` (Derived; the peak jerk of the reference $C^2$ polynomial).
* $\tau_{\text{delay}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` (Derived; observation age plus lease path plus brake onset, excluding $\Delta_{\text{da}}$).
* Drive limit `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` (Illustrative).

**Math**: The fixed allowances leave $D_{\text{avail}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_mm_str` $-$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.overhead_all_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_avail_str`. The jerk ramps lengthen the delay to $\tau' =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` $+$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ramp_delay_str` $=$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.tau_eff_str`, so $a_{\text{brake}}\tau' =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_str` m/s. Under the square root of @eq-enforce-speed-ceiling, $(a_{\text{brake}}\tau')^2 =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_sq_str` and $2a_{\text{brake}}D_{\text{avail}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.two_a_d_str` (both in m²/s²), whose sum has root `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.root_term_str` m/s; subtracting `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_tau_str` m/s gives the ceiling. At `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` the terms of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget sum to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.total_aisle_str`, and the remainder divided by the speed is the timing allowance.

**Result**: $v_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_str`, below the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit. The candidate aisle speed leaves `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` of spare, equivalent to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` of unallocated delay.

**Systems insight**: The irreversibility requirement $d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$, rather than motor electrical capability, dictates the operating speed. Running at the nominal drive limit violates the verified spatial budget, and the speed ceiling shifts strictly through the parameters governing the quadratic root and effective latency $\tau'$: available clearance, qualified braking deceleration, fixed margins, and end-to-end transport lag. Any latency introduced by downstream processing directly consumes the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` timing allowance, which cannot be arbitrarily replenished.

:::

We select `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` as a candidate transit speed below that ceiling. Its `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` margin is the sole clearance remaining to absorb unmodeled pipeline delays or provide secondary safety reserve.

This remaining margin is precariously narrow relative to the failure modes it must absorb. If chunk lease enforcement were entrusted to a non-real-time host operating system, an upstream planning stall lasting `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_stall_str` instead of the nominal `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.lease_ms_str` lease would inject `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.stall_added_str` of unbraked displacement, causing the base to overrun the rack clearance by `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.stall_breach_str`. This hazard underscores why lease termination must be autonomously enforced by dedicated microcontroller hardware directly gating motor power (@sec-enforcement-authority-refuse).

The sensor observation-age term terminates upon action dispatch, whereas the chunk lease takes effect upon admission. Between these milestones lies the dispatch-to-admission latency $\Delta_{\text{da}}$, cataloged as the second critical stage in the event ledger of @tbl-04-event-ledger. Because the baseline pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ excludes this transition, the complete operational delay expands to $\tau_{\mathrm{true}}=\tau_{\text{delay}}+\Delta_{\text{da}}$, requiring an additional spatial reservation of $v\Delta_{\text{da}}$. This phase encompasses any remaining neural inference, safety envelope projection, and inter-process communication; pipelined or overlapping stages must be budgeted carefully to avoid double-counting. A newly arrived sensor observation updates this ledger only when the hardware pipeline delivers and validates it prior to actuation. @Fig-12-capture-to-onset maps these sequential latencies onto a five-lane timing strip (camera, perception, proposal, permission, and drive) across time and physical travel, tracking how observation age and the hatched dispatch-to-admission interval lead up to lease expiry, MCU tick and bus transfer, and mechanical brake onset at the candidate aisle speed.

At this candidate speed, the unallocated timing allowance totals `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str`. To maintain a positive clearance reserve, elapsed time from capture to admission must not exceed `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_admission_max_str`, and total latency from capture to physical brake onset must stay strictly below `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_onset_max_str`. Operating at these precise boundaries exhausts all available clearance. These figures constitute formal qualification constraints rather than empirical performance claims. In @sec-placement-isolation-decisions, the architecture allocates $\Delta_{\text{da}} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_da_str` to the partitioned compute pipeline, consuming `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.travel_da_str` of the spatial margin while preserving a safety cushion of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_t_str` (equivalent to `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_d_str` of distance). Under this allocation, total latency from sensor capture to brake onset is `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_onset_str`. Because this parameter represents an engineering budget rather than an empirical measurement, the instrumented validation campaign in @sec-placement-testing-separation must verify it with physical hardware timestamps before the vehicle can be certified to operate at this speed. @Tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget and @fig-enforcement-stopping-budget break down this cumulative spatial expenditure across successive physical and computational layers: in the stacked bar chart, seven bars at the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit accumulate braking distance, sensor age, and communication overhead against the horizontal `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance threshold, showing how jerk-limited S-curve shaping (bar 6) and tracking insets (bar 7) force a severe clearance breach; in contrast, the eighth bar at the candidate `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` aisle speed preserves a positive `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.reserve_d_str` safety reserve.

: **The warehouse mobile manipulator's stopping budget**: Each numbered row details the distance contributed by a physical subsystem or software stage, modeled for a loaded chassis on a dry industrial floor at the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_drive_str` drive limit vs. the candidate `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` aisle speed; the running total and clearance remainder are evaluated at the drive limit against the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.d_clear_str` obstacle clearance. Row 6 accounts for the additional displacement imposed by jerk-limited $C^2$ deceleration profiles relative to ideal constant deceleration. Time-only rows contribute latency rather than physical distance. The totals exclude dispatch-to-admission displacement $v\,\Delta_{\text{da}}$, which must be absorbed by the remaining clearance budget at the chosen aisle speed. {#tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget tbl-colwidths="[5,17,38,10,10,10,10]"}

::: {#fig-enforcement-stopping-budget fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The stopping budget, row by row**: Each bar illustrates the cumulative distance required as each successive physical and timing term is incorporated into the budget, evaluated at the vehicle drive limit under loaded conditions on dry concrete. While kinematic braking, fixed margins, actuator onset, lease execution, and perception age collectively remain within the available clearance, the jerk-limited deceleration profile causes the total to exceed the boundary, and the closed-loop tracking inset exacerbates this overrun. The final bar displays the accounted subtotal at the candidate aisle speed, where the remaining clearance must absorb the dispatch-to-admission interval before providing a net safety reserve." fig-alt="Stacked bar chart of stopping distance in millimeters. Seven bars at the drive limit grow from braking alone to the full budget, adding overhead, brake onset, lease path, observation age, the matched stop suffix, and the tracking inset; the sixth and seventh bars cross a dashed horizontal line marking the clear distance at the rack end. An eighth bar at the aisle speed, built from the same terms, ends below the line."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE STOPPING BUDGET, ROW BY ROW (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-enforcement-stopping-budget
# │ Goal:    show each chapter's term accumulating against the clear distance
# │ Show:    seven stacked bars at the drive limit, one at the aisle speed,
# │          and the clear-distance line
# │ How:     the terms of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget from RM/AISLE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim import viz

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # category: derived (reference polynomial's peak jerk)
lease_path = AISLE.t_lease + AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus  # category: chosen (lease, tick) + illustrative (bus)
d_clear_mm = AISLE.d_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def terms(v):
    brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter).magnitude
    c2 = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter).magnitude
    return {
        "braking": brake,
        "overhead": (AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.delta_margin).to(millimeter).magnitude,
        "brake onset": (v * AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millimeter).magnitude,
        "lease path": (v * lease_path).to(millimeter).magnitude,
        "observation age": (v * AISLE.perception_age).to(millimeter).magnitude,
        "stop-suffix shape": c2 - brake,
        "tracking inset": AISLE.eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude,
    }

order = list(terms(v_drive).keys())
drive = terms(v_drive)
aisle = terms(v_aisle)
bars = [{k: (drive[k] if i <= n else 0.0) for i, k in enumerate(order)} for n in range(len(order))]
bars.append(aisle)
totals = [sum(b.values()) for b in bars]

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(totals[6] - 1163.8375) < 1e-6, "Row 7 total at the drive limit is 1163.84 mm.")
check(abs(totals[7] - 968.9925) < 1e-6, "The aisle-speed bar is 968.99 mm.")
check(totals[4] < d_clear_mm < totals[5], "The budget first passes the clear distance at row 6.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.6))
# Vol IV roles (tex/theme-colors.tex): structural pine for braking and its shape,
# authority purple for the lease path, measured petrol for observation age,
# neutral inks for fixed terms; red stays reserved for the clear-distance breach.
palette = {
    "braking": "#1A4D3E",
    "overhead": "#E2E8F0",
    "brake onset": "#4A5568",
    "lease path": "#5B4B8A",
    "observation age": "#007A87",
    "stop-suffix shape": "#8FB3A5",
    "tracking inset": "#A0AEC0",
}
labels = [
    "1\nbraking",
    "2\n+ overhead",
    "3\n+ onset",
    "4\n+ lease",
    "5\n+ age",
    "6\n+ $C^2$ stop",
    "7\n+ inset",
    f"aisle\n{v_aisle.to(meter / second).magnitude:.1f} m/s",
]
x = list(range(len(bars)))
bottoms = [0.0] * len(bars)
for k in order:
    heights = [b[k] for b in bars]
    ax.bar(x, heights, bottom=bottoms, width=0.66, color=palette[k], edgecolor="white", lw=0.6, label=k, zorder=3)
    bottoms = [bt + h for bt, h in zip(bottoms, heights)]
for xi, t in zip(x, totals):
    ax.text(xi, t + 18, f"{t:,.2f}".rstrip("0").rstrip("."), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], zorder=5)

ax.axhline(d_clear_mm, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.4, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=4)
ax.text(
    -0.45,
    d_clear_mm + 18,
    f"clear distance at the rack end, {d_clear_mm:,.0f} mm",
    color=COLORS["RedLine"],
    fontsize=8.5,
    ha="left",
    va="bottom",
    zorder=5,
)
ax.axvline(6.5, color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.text(3.0, 1440, f"drive limit, {v_drive.to(meter / second).magnitude:.1f} m/s", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS["primary"], ha="center", va="bottom")

ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(labels, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.6, len(bars) - 0.4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1520)
ax.set_ylabel("Stopping distance (mm)")
handles, leg_labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(handles[::-1], leg_labels[::-1], loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1.0), fontsize=8.5, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

::: {#fig-12-capture-to-onset fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**From capture to brake onset, in time and in travel**: The warehouse mobile manipulator's permission path at the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, drawn to scale from the exposure midpoint of the frame that first shows the hazard. The observation age of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_age_str` ends at dispatch; the hatched dispatch-to-admission interval is the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.delta_da_str` allocation @sec-placement makes, a budget that loaded measurement must still confirm; the lease, one tick, one bus cycle, and drive onset follow admission. The row beneath reads the same axis as travel, so the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_latest_str` timing allowance and the `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.spare_str` spare are one interval. Admission later than `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_admission_max_str`, or onset later than `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.capture_to_onset_max_str`, spends clearance the budget does not have. The jerk-limited stop that follows onset runs past the right edge." fig-alt="Timing strip with five lanes labeled camera, perception, proposal, permission, and drive over a time axis in milliseconds. Exposure and readout bars start the camera lane, an observation-age bar ends at a dispatch marker, a hatched dispatch-to-admission bar ends at an admission marker, a lease bar ends at lease expiry followed by a short tick and bus bar, and a drive-onset bar ends at brake onset, after which a solid stop bar runs off the right edge. A bracket over the strip marks the timing allowance from dispatch to a dashed latest-admission line; a second dashed line marks the latest onset. A travel row beneath converts the axis to millimeters and brackets the same interval as the spare distance."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAPTURE TO BRAKE ONSET (TIMING STRIP FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-12-capture-to-onset
# │ Goal:    show the permission path as time becoming distance, with the
# │          unallocated timing allowance and the spare as one interval
# │ Show:    exposure, readout, observation age, Delta_da (hatched), lease,
# │          tick, bus, onset, the jerk-limited stop; the allowance bracket and
# │          the latest admission and onset; travel at the aisle speed
# │ How:     viz.capture_to_onset_strip reads every duration from AISLE
# │          (Delta_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission); the allowance and the
# │          spare come from EnforcementStoppingBudget; the stop from
# │          calc_scurve_stop_time / _distance at the aisle speed
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_distance, calc_scurve_stop_time
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim import viz
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
S = EnforcementStoppingBudget

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v_aisle = S.v_aisle  # category: chosen
t_allow = S.t_latest  # category: derived (spare / v at the aisle speed)
spare = S.spare  # category: derived
t_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_aisle, S.a_brake, S.j_brake)  # category: derived
d_stop = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, S.a_brake, S.j_brake)  # category: derived

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
strip = viz.capture_to_onset_strip(AISLE, v_aisle, t_allowance=t_allow, spare=spare, stop_time=t_stop, stop_distance=d_stop, xlim=(-14, 262))
t_latest_adm = next(e.t for e in strip.events if e.label.startswith("latest admission"))
t_latest_onset = next(e.t for e in strip.events if e.label.startswith("latest onset"))

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_latest_adm - S.capture_to_admission_max.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's latest admission must match the budget cell.")
check(abs(t_latest_onset - S.capture_to_onset_max.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's latest onset must match the budget cell.")
check(AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission < t_allow, "The allocated Delta_da must fit inside the timing allowance.")
check(
    abs((spare / v_aisle).to(millisecond).magnitude - t_allow.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9,
    "The allowance and the spare are one interval at the aisle speed.",
)

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip)
plt.show()
```

:::

This baseline stopping model evaluates a stationary obstacle situated at distance $D_{\text{clear}}$, such as a dropped warehouse tote or a pedestrian who has stepped out from an aisle rack and stopped. Under this assumption, the hazard remains fixed from the instant braking begins. If, instead, a pedestrian continues walking toward the vehicle throughout the reaction and braking phases, the obstacle actively closes the safety gap from the opposing direction (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion). Sizing the budget to accommodate an ongoing pedestrian approach would restrict the mobile base to a maximum speed of just `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_walk_str` at this rack end.

This drastic velocity reduction occurs because an active hazard penalizes the stopping budget by the *duration* of the stop rather than merely its displacement. Assuming an ISO 13855 approach velocity $v_h =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_human_str` across the entire reaction and stopping interval $\tau_{\text{delay}} + T_{\text{stop}}(v)$, the spatial budget acquires an additional closure penalty $v_h\,T_{\text{stop}}(v)$ absent from static calculations. When operating below the acceleration threshold $a_{\text{brake}}^2/j_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_plateau_str`, the jerk-limited braking profile cannot achieve peak deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$; it ramps deceleration up and immediately down in a triangular profile lasting $2\sqrt{v/j_{\max}}$. This duration diminishes far more slowly than the linear scaling $v/a_{\text{brake}}$ as velocity decreases. Initiating a jerk-limited stop from `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_walk_str` requires `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_stop_walk_str`, compared to only `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.t_stop_walk_const_str` for idealized step deceleration. While the mobile base travels only `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.brake_walk_str` during braking, the pedestrian advances `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.closure_walk_str` toward the robot over the same window. Achieving peak deceleration from such low speeds would demand a jerk of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.jerk_rescaled_walk_str`, vastly exceeding the mechanical qualification of the payload suspension; unconstrained step deceleration would permit `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.v_walk_const_str`. Consequently, jerk limits impose negligible spatial overhead at full aisle velocity but consume an overwhelming share of available clearance at low speeds—demonstrating why simply reducing operating speed yields diminishing safety returns against moving pedestrians.

Throttling nominal aisle velocity to the walking-person ceiling would severely degrade warehouse transport throughput for an event that facility layout and procedural crossing rules can prevent. The baseline operational design therefore mandates enforced physical or optical crossing restrictions at aisle ends, while the safety case register in @sec-frontier-residual-claims-register tracks the governing premise: that pedestrian incursions into the stopping zone are procedurally prevented.
