Placing a monitor on a separate physical core or processor does not establish true independence if that monitor shares a power rail, a memory bus, a sensor link, or an unisolated clock domain with the untrusted proposer. Shared hardware resources require provably bounded interference or a qualified, survivable fallback state. Any environmental condition that the monitor cannot observe directly must remain an explicit, documented operating premise rather than an unstated assumption.
:::

The runtime permission path is not the machine's certified functional safety layer; apart from a narrow hardware watchdog, its software checks carry no formal safety rating. Beneath this permission layer sit the certified safety functions embedded within motor drives, safety laser scanners, and the dedicated safety controller. These hardware-interlocked mechanisms carry the formal integrity claims that certification bodies audit against industrial standards. The primary operational duty of the software permission path is to regulate the learned proposer proactively so that the robot never trips those certified hardware interlocks during normal operation. @Sec-enforcement-certified-functions maps each dynamic response developed throughout this chapter onto that underlying certified safety floor once the complete response hierarchy is established.

### Where the thesis bends {#sec-enforcement-thesis-bends}

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-torque-policy
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A LEARNED POLICY AS THE CONTROL-RATE CONTROLLER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the "where the thesis bends" paragraphs immediately below.
# │ Goal:    price what the lease row of the stopping budget becomes when the
# │          policy itself emits a command every tick.
# │ Show:    lease-path travel at the aisle speed for the chunk lease and for a
# │          per-tick command stream.
# │ How:     AISLE lease, tick, and bus fields (rows 4 of the stopping budget).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementTorquePolicy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_row = (v_aisle * (t_lease + t_tick + t_bus)).to(millimeter)
    tick_row = (v_aisle * (t_tick + t_bus)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(lease_row.magnitude - 80.6) < 1e-6, "The chunk-lease row is 80.6 mm at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(abs(tick_row.magnitude - 2.6) < 1e-6, "A per-tick command stream leaves 2.6 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    lease_row_str = fmt_length(lease_row, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    tick_row_str = fmt_length(tick_row, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The primary machine architecture modeled in this chapter assigns kinematic intent to the learned policy while delegating closed-loop torque synthesis to deterministic motor drives. Much of contemporary robot learning practice, however, abandons this classical division. Modern learned locomotion controllers frequently output joint targets directly at the control rate, leaving only stiff joint-level proportional-derivative loops beneath them [@lee2020learning], while end-to-end torque policies eliminate even that intermediate layer. The foundational rule that a proposal is not permission (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}) does not disappear in such direct control designs. Instead, the range of physical guarantees that the runtime permission path can uphold narrows, and this narrowing occurs in precise, quantifiable ways.

Four essential guarantees survive because each acts directly on raw commands at the causal boundary without requiring a forward plan. First, a per-tick rate and amplitude limit bounds torque slew and joint velocity at the hardware register interface. Second, the kinetic barrier of @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque operates directly in effort space: because its safe half-space is written natively in torque, a control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP) filters the policy's output without converting it to an intermediate kinematic setpoint. Third, the passivity-based energy tank of @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact monitors power exchange and bounds the physical work the policy can inject into the environment during contact. Fourth, low-level geofencing, safely-limited speed monitoring, and torque removal backed by mechanical spring brakes remain permanently active underneath the software stack. Communication timing even improves along one critical dimension: because a per-tick policy stream issues updates every control cycle, watchdogs detect policy silence within a single tick plus bus transport delay, reducing the lease-expiration travel row of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget from `{python} EnforcementTorquePolicy.lease_row_str` to `{python} EnforcementTorquePolicy.tick_row_str` at the aisle speed.

What is lost is admission. Without an explicit multi-step trajectory, the system cannot verify a collision-free stopping suffix before the robot commits to motion. The enforcer must instead evaluate the machine's dynamic stopping reservation on every tick against an active fallback controller that maintains its own internal braking model. On a wheeled mobile base, that fallback is straightforward to formulate: the controller commands maximum service braking along the current heading or locks the wheel drives. On an underactuated balancing machine, such as a bipedal humanoid, the fallback is itself an active balance controller; cutting motor torque produces an immediate uncontrolled fall rather than a safe state.

Runtime projection also alters the closed sensorimotor loop under which the policy was trained. Every time the enforcer projects a proposed action onto the admissible set, it delivers a state to the environment that the policy never intended, precipitating distributional shift in subsequent observations. This penalty surfaces directly in task performance, as quantified by the intervention metrics of @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention. Frequent overrides cause the machine to chatter erratically along safety boundaries or freeze conservatively short of its goal. To reconcile this tension, modern architectures adopt filter-aware policy training, incorporating the safety filter directly into the training objective so that the neural network learns to avoid the boundary rather than encountering the enforcer for the first time on physical hardware [@hsu2024safetyfilter]. The core thesis still holds at the causal boundary: untrusted proposals never bypass runtime enforcement. What bends is how much of the safety argument can be settled mathematically before motion begins vs. how much performance the machine must sacrifice to settle the remainder while moving.
## The Fallback Ladder {#sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder}

A safety filter must select its fallback before the admissible control set becomes empty. Once that set is empty, no control input can guarantee forward invariance; a fallback can mitigate damage or contain a fault, but it cannot prevent a boundary crossing. Furthermore, physical systems cannot rely on a single, binary kill switch. Abruptly severing DC bus power whenever a control proposal approaches a barrier boundary induces uncontrolled deceleration, mechanical shock, and incessant false-positive mission aborts. Conversely, attempting to execute complex software optimization during a catastrophic hardware fault—such as an inverter shoot-through (@sec-body-actuator-limits)—destroys gate driver FETs milliseconds before an interrupt handler can even dispatch.

To resolve these competing physical realities, the permission path maintains a deterministic ladder of resident protective responses. The runtime arbiter evaluates plant kinematics, remaining sensor validity, and hardware integrity on every control cycle, selecting deterministically among minimally invasive projection, closed-loop position holding, controlled deceleration, or complete torque removal.

::: {#dfn-enforcement-dynamic-fallback-ladder .callout-definition title="Dynamic fallback ladder"}

***Dynamic fallback ladder***\index{Dynamic fallback ladder!definition}\index{Fallback ladder!definition} is the set of resident protective responses ($\mathbf{u} \in \{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}), \mathbf{u}_{\text{hold}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{stop}}, \mathbf{u}_{\text{cutoff}}\}$) from which a deterministic arbiter selects one on every tick according to the check that failed (an invariant violation, a timing overrun, or a hardware fault) and the measured state of the plant, so that one trigger can select different rungs in motion and at standstill.

1.  **Significance**: Physical AI systems cannot treat all faults identically. Cutting actuator power on dynamic, underactuated, or high-momentum plants (for example, legged robots mid-stride or multirotors in flight) precipitates immediate catastrophic falls or tumbling. These platforms require state-matched active deceleration before executing terminal torque removal.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike software exception handlers that unwind the call stack or terminate a user-space thread, a dynamic fallback ladder operates against physical momentum. The arbiter matches each rung to the remaining valid sensor channels, surviving control authority, and available stopping clearance.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the rungs as an escalation sequence where lower rungs, such as Safe Torque Off (STO), inherently provide faster or safer arrest. Each rung possesses distinct entry prerequisites; invoking an unpowered torque inhibit on an airborne drone or an unbraked mobile base allows the machine to coast freely without arresting motion.

:::

### The four-rung operational hierarchy {#sec-enforcement-four-rungs}

The dynamic fallback architecture organizes protection across four resident responses: PROJECT, HOLD, STOP, and INHIBIT. Each response executes on the specific compute and actuation substrate that survives the initiating trigger. The deterministic arbiter does not traverse these rungs sequentially like an exception escalation cascade; instead, it samples measured plant state (velocity, position, payload loading) and fault severity on every millisecond tick to dispatch the surviving actuation and sensing substrate directly:

1. `PROJECT`, minimal-intervention projection in MCU firmware. The primary safety filter executes on every control cycle while the feasible control set is nonempty ($\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}} \neq \emptyset$), the proposal lease is fresh, and tracking error remains within bounds ($\|e(t)\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$). It computes the minimal-intervention torque $\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u}} \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}\|^2$ subject to active barrier half-spaces within its `{python} EnforcementCycleBudget.qp_us_str` $\mu\text{s}$ cycle allocation. It makes the smallest feasible effort correction under the stated invariance assumptions; the planner must still account for any changed task-space path.
2. `HOLD`, powered hold at standstill in MCU firmware. When the machine is stationary, the arbiter selects an energized position hold, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 2 stop: Safe Stop 2 (SS2) followed by Safe Operating Stop (SOS), the drive function that monitors standstill.[^fn-stop-category-iec60204] Its protective validity stems from that certified standstill monitor rather than the position loop gain. Because IEC 60204-1 permits only Category 0 or Category 1 for an emergency stop, HOLD can never serve as an E-stop response [@iec60204]. The drives maintain coordinate $\mathbf{x}_{\text{hold}}$ under closed-loop position control, modulating inverter phase currents against gravity and static loads. While this rung incurs continuous Joule heating in motor windings\index{Joule heating} (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), it eliminates friction brake wear and preserves kinematic calibration, enabling instantaneous task resumption when a valid trajectory proposal arrives. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, this rung handles lapsed leases or lost host heartbeats specifically when the platform is already at standstill.
3. `STOP`, controlled dynamic stop in MCU firmware. When a machine in active transit loses proposal authority, tracking error diverges, or an obstacle breaches the stopping envelope, the response is a resident, state-matched controlled stop, analogous to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop (Safe Stop 1 / SS1). Its certified counterpart is the ramp-monitored variant (SS1-r), which checks deceleration against a bounded profile throughout the arrest; the unmonitored, time-controlled variant (SS1-t) merely removes torque after a fixed delay without verifying that the planned $C^2$ ramp actually decelerated the load [@iec61800part52]. The resident $C^2$ quartic position suffix serves this role provided the entry state falls within its validated domain. Executed autonomously by bare-metal MCU firmware directly from local SRAM, this stop peaks at the credible deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$, returning kinetic energy through motor inverters to the DC bus for absorption by the qualified regeneration path. Power removal and mechanical brake clamping occur only after confirmed zero velocity.
4. `INHIBIT`, torque inhibit and spring-brake clamping by hardware interlocks. When the safety microcontroller suffers a brownout, clock loss, or watchdog timeout, all software decision logic ceases. Dedicated, out-of-band hardware interlocks trigger Safe Torque Off (STO) to de-energize gate drive power supplies and drop hold current to electromechanical spring-applied brakes. This terminal rung removes motor torque without software intervention; the mechanical brakes provide only their independently qualified holding or dynamic stopping capacity.

[^fn-stop-category-iec60204]: **Machine Stop Categories**\index{IEC 60204-1!Stopping categories}\index{Functional safety!Emergency stop categories}: IEC 60204-1 distinguishes uncontrolled power removal (Category 0), controlled stopping followed by power removal (Category 1), and controlled stopping with power retained (Category 2). A category defines electrical power status rather than stopping distance; every rung therefore requires its own empirically validated stopping measurement.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-stop-rung
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE STOP RUNG ON THE MACHINE'S BASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the controlled-stop paragraph immediately below.
# │ Goal:    show that the stop rung executes the resident C2 suffix.
# │ Show:    aisle speed, credible deceleration, suffix duration and distance.
# │ How:     calc_scurve_stop_time / _distance on AISLE.v_aisle and
# │          AISLE.a_brake; jerk bound from calc_c2_stop_suffix at the drive limit.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance, calc_scurve_stop_time
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementStopRung:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # reference polynomial's peak jerk
    duration = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    distance = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(duration.magnitude - 931.25) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s takes 931.25 ms.")
    check(abs(distance.magnitude - 605.3125) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s covers 605.31 mm.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    duration_str = fmt_latency(duration, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    distance_str = fmt_length(distance, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
```

When a machine in motion loses proposal authority or violates a tracking bound, the arbiter engages a controlled dynamic stop, operating analogously to an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 stop\index{Safe stop 1}. On the warehouse mobile manipulator base, this rung executes the resident stop suffix pre-admitted alongside the motion trajectory (@sec-planning-behavior-seam), rather than attempting to synthesize a stopping trajectory on the fly during a fault. In steady-state cruising with zero acceleration, this pre-computed profile seamlessly matches the operating state at fault onset; nonzero acceleration states require their own qualified state-matched suffixes. From an aisle cruise velocity of `{python} EnforcementStopRung.v_aisle_str`, the jerk-limited $C^2$ suffix sustains a credible peak deceleration of `{python} EnforcementStopRung.a_brake_str` between its jerk transitions. The entire maneuver spans `{python} EnforcementStopRung.duration_str` and traverses `{python} EnforcementStopRung.distance_str`—the exact braking margin reserved in the stopping envelope calculations of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes. Because the deceleration phase channels kinetic energy back through the inverter into the DC bus (@sec-body-power-integrity), bus capacitance and braking choppers must absorb this regenerative surge without triggering a bus overvoltage fault. Complete electrical power removal, if mandated by protocol, occurs only after sensors verify standstill.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-rail-holdup
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL AND THE UNBUDGETED INHIBIT RUNG
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the inhibit paragraph immediately below.
# │ Goal:    compare logic/coil hold-up with the selected stop sequence;
# │          inverter torque survival is a separate qualification premise.
# │ Show:    spring-brake engage range, hold-up, flag-to-brakes-set time, margin.
# │ How:     RM D15 rail fields; the S-curve suffix at the inspected-floor
# │          ceiling (EnforcementStoppingBudget) with the friction-bound peak
# │          and the load's jerk bound.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_time
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementRailHoldup:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen
    engage_min = RM.spring_brake_engage_min  # category: illustrative
    engage_max = RM.spring_brake_engage_max  # category: illustrative
    tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    a_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_inspected  # category: derived (mu_inspected_floor * g)
    v_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_inspected  # category: derived (inspected-floor ceiling)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    flag_to_onset = (tick + bus + onset).to(millisecond)
    longest_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_inspected, a_inspected, EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake).to(millisecond)
    flag_to_set = (flag_to_onset + longest_stop + engage_max).to(millisecond)
    margin = (holdup - flag_to_set).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "The permission rail holds up for 2.0 s.")
    check(abs(flag_to_onset.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "Stop onset follows the flag within 22 ms.")
    check(abs(flag_to_set.magnitude - 1313.43) < 5e-3, "Flag to all brakes set is 1313.43 ms.")
    check(abs(margin.magnitude - 686.57) < 5e-3, "The hold-up leaves 686.57 ms.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    engage_min_ms_str = fmt_latency(engage_min, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    engage_max_ms_str = fmt_latency(engage_max, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    holdup_str = fmt_latency(holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
    flag_to_onset_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    longest_stop_str = fmt_latency(longest_stop, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    flag_to_set_str = fmt_latency(flag_to_set, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    margin_str = fmt_latency(margin, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
```

Beyond firmware-driven stops, a separate out-of-band circuit can inhibit motor torque generation entirely. Drive Safe Torque Off (STO) cuts gate-drive bias to isolate inverter FETs, but it does not disconnect the DC bus, energize mechanical friction brakes, or actively decelerate a moving rotor; an unbraked motor will simply coast under its existing momentum. In robust architectures, an external safety controller simultaneously drives a separately rated contactor and spring-applied mechanical brakes. Engineers must evaluate the dynamic stopping distance of this combined pathway as an integrated system, because dropping drive torque while an arm is under gravitational load or while a vehicle is at speed can exacerbate the hazard. For the warehouse mobile manipulator, this pathway—combining STO with nine spring brakes engaging between `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_min_ms_str` and `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_max_ms_str` following coil flux decay—constitutes the unbudgeted INHIBIT rung. It serves exclusively as a hardware backstop for MCU cycle failure, and the primary stopping envelope claims do not rely on it.

An undervoltage fault on the shared drive bus can invoke the STOP rung only while inverter gate drives, angular encoders, and control logic retain adequate voltage for closed-loop deceleration. The isolated permission rail (@sec-body-archetype-matrix) maintains power to logic circuits, transceivers, and brake coils for `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.holdup_str`, but it does not supply the motor currents required for braking torque. Consequently, timing guarantees for powered stopping assume a surviving drive bus. Under this condition, dynamic braking begins within `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.flag_to_onset_str` of the fault flag; stopping from the inspected-floor speed ceiling of `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_inspected_str` requires `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.longest_stop_str`; and mechanical brake engagement at standstill adds at most `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.engage_max_ms_str`. This entire sequence completes within `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.flag_to_set_str`, preserving a `{python} EnforcementRailHoldup.margin_str` buffer of control logic hold-up.

This analysis confirms the control-supply duration budget, whereas the electrical drive-energy budget requires separate qualification. Systems engineers must prove through empirical testing that the DC bus capacitance, inverter power stages, and regenerative dump resistors sustain controlled deceleration under worst-case electrical fault conditions. If the drive stage cannot guarantee this power integrity, the system must either adopt an unpowered dynamic braking configuration or restrict its operational safety envelope; INHIBIT cannot be credited with standard Category 1 stopping performance. Similarly, at standstill, an undervoltage fault must trigger verified mechanical brake engagement before the logic supply decays, rather than attempting to maintain an active HOLD indefinitely on finite capacitance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Hardware trip zones and dynamic braking are introduced in @sec-nervous-actuation-authority.
:::

Physical AI systems engineers must distinguish between **fail-safe** and **fail-operational** plants when configuring terminal fallbacks. In a machine already at a mechanically restrained standstill, removing drive torque is safe once mechanical engagement is verified. On underactuated, open-loop unstable, or high-momentum platforms, however, abruptly removing actuator torque directly initiates a catastrophic failure mode:

1. **Aerial platforms (multirotors and eVTOLs)**: Cutting motor torque drops aerodynamic thrust to zero instantly, transforming an airborne vehicle into an uncontrolled ballistic projectile.
2. **Dynamic legged systems (bipedal humanoids)**: During dynamic locomotion, the robot's center of mass frequently falls outside the support polygon; stability depends on active ground-reaction forces and momentum exchange. Suddenly removing joint torques causes an unrecoverable fall, with impact severity governed by gait phase and available compliance.
3. **High-speed autonomous vehicles**: De-energizing steering actuators or electric traction motors at highway speeds strips away the control authority required to execute a coordinated deceleration, leaving the vehicle at the mercy of passive road friction.

The physical channel that dispatches a hardware torque-removal request is the out-of-band interlock described in @sec-nervous-actuation-authority. @Fig-12-estop-interlock diagrams how an industrial emergency-stop circuit distributes authority across three hardware stages to guarantee fault tolerance while isolating the spring-applied brake on its own dedicated current loop: in Stage 1, a positive-break mushroom pushbutton opens redundant $S_1/S_2$ normally closed contacts; in Stage 2, dual force-guided safety relays ($K_1/K_2$) couple drive enable lines with External Device Monitoring (EDM) series feedback to lock out restart upon contact weld; in Stage 3, separate outputs de-energize drive Safe Torque Off (STO) inverter inputs ($\tau = 0$) while an independent de-energized current loop drops magnetic flux to set the spring-applied mechanical shaft brake. This physical separation enforces the principle that removing drive torque ($\tau = 0$) and arresting physical momentum are distinct functions requiring separate validation paths:

1.  **Dual-channel E-stop ingress (Stage 1):** The physical mushroom pushbutton operates two mechanically linked, normally closed (NC) contact sets ($S_1$ and $S_2$). Depressing the button breaks both channels simultaneously. Using two separate channels ensures that a single short-circuit or contact weld across one pair cannot prevent the circuit from opening.
2.  **Redundant safety relays with External Device Monitoring (Stage 2):** Two force-guided safety relays ($K_1$ and $K_2$) monitor the dual channels. Each relay couples its primary normally open (NO) drive-enabling contacts with a mechanically linked, normally closed External Device Monitoring (EDM) contact. If one relay's contacts weld shut due to an electrical surge, its EDM contact remains held open, preventing the safety circuit from resetting and alerting the supervisor to the hidden hardware failure.
3.  **Separate stop functions (Stage 3):** De-energizing the safety relays drives two physically independent outputs. The drive's Safe Torque Off (STO) input de-energizes the gate drive power supply for the three-phase inverter bridge, rendering the power MOSFETs or IGBTs high-impedance, so the motor can no longer produce electromagnetic torque. As the diagram highlights, STO alone does not apply mechanical braking: an unbraked motor carries momentum and may coast freely. A separate coil circuit powers the spring-applied electromechanical friction brake. When power is removed, coil magnetic flux decays, allowing internal springs to physically clamp friction pads against the motor shaft, applying the brake without electrical power. A holding-brake rating does not establish the ability to arrest a moving load; dynamic stopping requires separate energy, torque, and response qualification.

::: {#fig-12-estop-interlock fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative emergency-stop circuit**: The three stages map to the numbered list above. Two linked contacts each hold a force-guided relay, the relays' enable contacts hold the drive's two Safe Torque Off (STO) inputs, and their EDM contacts in series block a restart after a weld. The spring-applied brake runs on its own supply, and a supply contactor, if fitted, provides galvanic disconnection. A moving motor can coast after STO, so the brake's set time and the physical stopping distance must be measured for the load and state." fig-alt="Two-channel schematic in three labeled stages. Stage 1, dual-channel E-stop: a red positive-break E-stop mechanically linked to normally closed contacts S1 and S2, each fed from 24 volts. Stage 2, redundant relays with EDM: S1 drives the coil of force-guided relay K1 and S2 the coil of K2; each relay has a normally open enable contact and a normally closed EDM contact, and the EDM contacts in series run with a dashed teal line to a reset monitor, restart only if K1 and K2 released. Stage 3, separate stop functions: K1 and K2 send STO1 and STO2 enable to the drive, whose gate-drive supply feeds an inverter bridge driving motor M, tagged in red tau equals 0 and noted may coast. A dashed box above the drive reads supply contactor, if fitted. A brake supply on its own circuit, via K1 and K2, feeds a spring brake that clamps on power loss and acts on the motor shaft, with a dashed tag reading brake set time: measure."}
![](images/svg/fig12_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The necessity of hardwired, out-of-band trip circuits is underscored by the catastrophic history of replacing electromechanical safety interlocks with software logic (\ref{ws-enforcement-therac-25-software-interlock-elimination}).

::: {#ws-enforcement-therac-25-software-interlock-elimination .callout-war-story title="Therac-25 software interlock elimination"}
**Context**: Between 1985 and 1987, the Therac-25 medical linear accelerator administered massive radiation overdoses to six cancer patients after system designers eliminated the electromechanical interlocks used in previous models, assigning safety-critical beam containment entirely to software [@leveson1993investigating].

**Mechanism**: Software race conditions and shared memory corruption in the operator interface allowed the machine to fire its high-current electron beam (25 MeV) without rotating the tungsten target and beam-flattening filter into position. Because the physical microswitches that previously interlocked beam activation had been removed, the underlying hardware possessed no independent means to detect that the operational mode conflicted with the turntable state.

**Impact**: Six patients received radiation doses estimated between 4,000 and 20,000 rads (up to 100 times the therapeutic level), causing severe tissue necrosis and three direct fatalities [@leveson1993investigating].

**Response**: Investigators mandated the restoration of independent hardware interlocks, requiring positive electromechanical verification of turntable configuration prior to beam generation, alongside formal software safety lifecycle standards.

**Systems lesson**: A software-based protection layer cannot serve as its own independent backstop. A runtime barrier filter may exercise binding authority over nominal control proposals, but the architecture still requires an out-of-band, physically independent trip mechanism to survive processor lockups, memory corruption, and firmware bugs. Moreover, because torque removal alone does not guarantee deceleration, the surviving physical response must match the plant's dynamic envelope.
:::

@Fig-12-fallback-ladder formalizes these four terminal rungs across firmware and hardware execution paths: three software rungs (`PROJECT`, `HOLD`, and `STOP`) evaluate inside Safety MCU firmware ($1\text{ kHz}$ tick), routing through an arbiter multiplexer that selects a single valid actuation command $\mathbf{u}_{\text{act}}$ for the drives, while the fourth rung (`INHIBIT`) bypasses firmware entirely along an out-of-band hardware interlock that cuts inverter gate power (STO) and drops spring-brake holding current upon processor failure or critical sensor loss. The rungs trade response latency, control authority, and recovery overhead against one another, selecting directly among responses whose physical and computational entry prerequisites remain valid. A controlled stop demands verified drive electronics and sufficient stopping clearance; losing drive integrity forces immediate fallback to unpowered mitigation strategies that carry strictly weaker physical guarantees.

::: {#fig-12-fallback-ladder fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Fallback responses and the paths that run them**: The plant state and the failed check select one response directly; the four are alternatives, not steps of an escalation. PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP run in the safety MCU's firmware and reach the drives through its arbiter, which here passes the projected command. INHIBIT is the one response that survives loss of the MCU itself, so it bypasses the arbiter on a hardware path that removes gate-drive supply and lets the spring brakes set. On a moving machine that path also removes motor braking, and the machine coasts until the separately qualified brakes take hold." fig-alt="Four rows, each with a condition card on the left joined by an arrow to a response card. The first three responses, PROJECT, HOLD, and STOP, sit inside a dashed box labeled safety MCU firmware, 1 kHz, and feed a multiplexer whose selected input, PROJECT, connects to an output arrow labeled u act entering a tall box labeled drives and brakes. The fourth response, INHIBIT, sits in a separate dashed box labeled hardware interlock and connects directly to the drives box by an arrow labeled STO, brake supply. The PROJECT condition, proposal u nom admitted, is drawn dashed in bronze."}
![](images/svg/fig12_canonical_fallback_ladder.svg){width="100%"}
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-incident-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TEMPE AND CRUISE RECORDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the Cruise war story below, the Tempe pitfall, and
# │          @fig-12-uber-tempe-timeline.
# │ Goal:    print the investigators' values instead of hand-typed literals.
# │ Show:    Tempe first detection 5.6 s and recognition 1.2 s before impact;
# │          Cruise pullover about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up to 7.7 mph (3.4 m/s).
# │ How:     literature values from NTSB/HAR-19/03 and the Quinn Emanuel
# │          report, the same values as @sec-boundary-when-fails loads, kept
# │          here until the literature registry holds them.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

class EnforcementIncidentRecord:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019), p. v and table pp. 15-16
    t_detect = 5.6 * second  # first detection, before impact
    t_recognize = 1.2 * second  # imminent collision recognized, before impact
    # category: literature. Quinn Emanuel report to the Cruise boards (2024), p. 10
    d_drag = 20 * ureg.foot  # approximate distance moved during the pullover
    v_drag = 7.7 * ureg.mph  # maximum speed during the pullover

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_drag_m = d_drag.to(meter)
    v_drag_ms = v_drag.to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_recognize < t_detect, "Recognition comes after first detection.")
    # fig-12-uber-tempe-timeline fig-alt hand-types 5.6 s and 1.2 s.
    check(abs(t_detect.magnitude - 5.6) < 1e-9 and abs(t_recognize.magnitude - 1.2) < 1e-9, "The NTSB times are 5.6 s and 1.2 s.")
    check(abs(d_drag_m.magnitude - 6.096) < 1e-3, "20 ft is 6.1 m.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_recognize_str = fmt_latency(t_recognize, unit=second, precision=1)
    d_drag_str = fmt_length(d_drag, unit=ureg.foot, precision=0)
    d_drag_m_str = fmt_length(d_drag_m, unit=meter, precision=1)
    v_drag_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag, unit=ureg.mph, precision=1)
    v_drag_ms_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag_ms, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

::: {#ws-enforcement-cruise-fallback-dragging .callout-war-story title="Cruise post-impact fallback (2023)"}
**Context**: In October 2023, an autonomous Cruise robotaxi in San Francisco encountered a pedestrian who had been struck by an adjacent human-driven vehicle and propelled into the robotaxi's travel lane [@exponent2024cruise].

**Mechanism**: The autonomous vehicle initiated an immediate emergency stop upon detecting the impact. However, the collision-classification subsystem erroneously localized the pedestrian to the side of the vehicle rather than under the chassis, categorizing the event as a side collision. The operational design domain for side collisions specified a secondary pullover maneuver to clear traffic. Because the perception pipeline had tracked the pedestrian only intermittently before the collision, the tracker marked the lane ahead as clear, prompting the vehicle to accelerate from standstill into the pullover [@exponent2024cruise].

**Impact**: Executing the pullover dragged the pedestrian—who remained pinned beneath the vehicle's floorpan—approximately `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.d_drag_str` (`{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.d_drag_m_str`) at speeds reaching `{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.v_drag_str` (`{python} EnforcementIncidentRecord.v_drag_ms_str`), causing severe trauma [@quinnemanuel2024cruise]. The California DMV subsequently suspended Cruise's autonomous testing and deployment permits, prompting Cruise to halt fleet operations nationwide and recall software across 950 vehicles [@cadmv2023cruise; @exponent2024cruise].

**Response**: A post-collision fallback must prohibit renewed motion whenever state uncertainty persists. In this scenario, retaining a locked standstill and mandating physical inspection prevents the system from treating missing perceptual tracks as free space. Teleoperation feeds cannot substitute for verified local sensor coverage.

**Systems lesson**: An embodied fallback cannot infer free space from the absence of sensor tracks. Every transition across fallback states requires positive evidence verifying that assumed physical invariants hold, paired with failsafe physical restraints while state ambiguity remains unresolved.
:::

### Industrial stop categories and the safe torque off trap {#sec-enforcement-stop-categories}

Decelerating the mobile manipulator uses closed-loop motor torque during the active braking phase, engaging mechanical holding brakes only once the plant reaches confirmed standstill. Industrial standards distinguish machine-level stop categories from drive-level safety functions across this sequence. Standard IEC 60204-1 classifies whether electrical power remains connected during and after deceleration, whereas functional safety standards such as IEC 61800-5-2 define specific drive functions—including Safe Torque Off (STO), Safe Stop 1 (SS1), and Safe Stop 2 (SS2)—that execute individual stages of a response. @Tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories maps these formal classifications to their concrete physical obligations.

| Response                                                    | Motor torque and power                                                         | Physical stop obligation                                                                           | Appropriate use                                          |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Admitted filtering                                          | Drive remains active                                                           | Recheck the feasible kinetic barrier and tracking bound every tick                                 | Nominal operation inside the validated envelope          |
| Controlled hold (Category 2 / SS2-like)                     | Power remains for braking and hold                                             | Verify stopping distance, thermal headroom, and static load support                                | Hold when feedback and torque authority remain available |
| Controlled stop then torque removal (Category 1 / SS1-like) | Power remains through deceleration; torque is removed afterward                | Verify the full braking and transition time under load                                             | Moving machine with enough reserved clearance            |
| Torque removal (Category 0 / STO-like)                      | Drive cannot produce commanded torque; DC bus isolation is a separate function | A moving motor may coast; a separate brake or mechanical restraint needs its own timing and rating | State for which loss of torque has been shown safe       |

: **Stop functions and physical response**: Machine stop categories, related drive functions, and the plant response each leaves to be tested. No stop category alone supplies a safety integrity rating, a brake, galvanic isolation, or a guaranteed stopping distance. {#tbl-12-iec60204-stopping-categories tbl-colwidths="[18,21,34,27]"}

### Certified safety functions beneath the permission path {#sec-enforcement-certified-functions}

In an embodied deployment, not all firmware executing the fallback ladder carries formal functional safety certification. A certification engineer immediately partitions software claims by the integrity of the underlying hardware substrate. On a production machine, formal guarantees rest primarily on a second, lower layer: dedicated safety functions in the motor drives, the optical safety scanner, and the arm's safety controller, each architected and validated to a Performance Level (PL) under ISO 13849-1 (@sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning) [@iso13849part1]. These hardened functions substantiate the certified protective envelope. Above them, the MCU permission path operates primarily as an unrated performance layer designed to keep the learned policy inside the admissible set, preventing unnecessary trips of the hard safety floor. Only one narrow component of this MCU layer requires safety qualification: the hardware watchdog and heartbeat monitor that revokes authority when lease renewals cease.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-certified-functions
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE ARM'S ROBOT CLASS AND ITS SPEED-AND-SEPARATION DISTANCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the certified-functions table and the arm SSM paragraph below.
# │ Goal:    classify the arm under ISO 10218-1:2025 and evaluate the terms of the
# │          SSM protective separation distance that the chapter already owns.
# │ Show:    arm mass against the Class I limit; S_h, S_r, S_s and their sum;
# │          the human term's share.
# │ How:     RM.arm.mass; EnforcementAuthorityLoss (descending-joint stop);
# │          AISLE.tau_delay as the reaction time if the vision path were the
# │          separation sensor; AISLE.v_human_approach (ISO 13855 K).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementCertifiedFunctions:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    arm_mass = RM.arm.mass  # category: datasheet
    class1_mass = 10.0 * kilogram  # category: standard (ISO 10218-1:2025 Class I limit, per Hartmann et al. 2026)
    class1_speed = 0.25 * meter / second  # category: standard (ISO 10218-1:2025 Class I limit)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 K)
    t_r = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (vision-path delay; not a safety-rated sensing path)
    v_r = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.tcp_speed  # category: illustrative (descending tool point)
    omega = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed  # category: illustrative
    alpha_net = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.alpha_eff  # category: illustrative (bias-reduced)
    s_s = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_eff  # category: illustrative (biased tool stop)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_s = (omega / alpha_net).to(millisecond)
    s_h = (v_h * (t_r + t_s)).to(millimeter)
    s_r = (v_r * t_r).to(millimeter)
    s_partial = (s_h + s_r + s_s).to(millimeter)
    share_h = (s_h / s_partial).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(arm_mass > class1_mass, "The registered arm exceeds the Class I mass limit, so it is Class II.")
    check(v_r > class1_speed, "The descending tool point also exceeds the Class I speed limit.")
    check(abs(t_s.magnitude - 165.517) < 5e-3, "The biased joint stop takes about 166 ms.")
    check(share_h > 0.6, "The person's own approach dominates the separation distance.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    arm_mass_str = fmt(arm_mass.to(kilogram).magnitude, precision=0)
    class1_mass_str = fmt(class1_mass.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_s_str = fmt_latency(round(t_s.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_r_str = fmt_latency(t_r, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_h_str = fmt_velocity(v_h, precision=1)
    v_r_str = fmt_velocity(v_r, precision=2)
    s_h_str = fmt_length(round(s_h.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    s_r_str = fmt_length(round(s_r.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    s_s_str = fmt_length(round(s_s.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    s_partial_str = fmt_length(round(s_partial.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    share_h_str = fmt_percent(round(share_h, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
```

@Tbl-12-certified-functions maps each response and speed channel onto its certified industrial counterpart. The core drive functions derive from IEC 61800-5-2 [@iec61800part52]: **safe torque off (STO)**, **safe stop 1 (SS1)**, **safe stop 2 (SS2)**, **safe operating stop (SOS)** (which monitors standstill), **safely limited speed (SLS)**, and **safe brake control (SBC)** (which drives the mechanical brake coil through a monitored output). For the mobile base, ISO 3691-4 assigns required performance level (PLr) d to braking system control and personnel detection within the travel path, while assigning PLr b to the electromechanical parking brake [@iso3691part4; @tuv2021iso3691]. For robotic manipulators, ISO 10218-1:2025 classifies systems into Class I (manipulator mass under `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.class1_mass_str` kg with strictly limited force and velocity) and Class II, mandating PL d (or SIL 2) across all safety functions on Class II arms [@iso10218part1; @hartmann2026evolution]. Because the warehouse arm weighs `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.arm_mass_str` kg, it is governed by Class II mandates.

| Response or channel                  | Certified counterpart                                        | Governing requirement                               | Required level on this machine                      |
|:-------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------|
| `PROJECT`, feasibility, evidence-age | None; the admission checks are not claimed as safety rated   | None                                                | None claimed; recorded as a premise                 |
| Lease expiry and heartbeat loss      | MCU watchdog that commands STO or SS1 on the drives          | ISO 13849-1; IEC 61508 for the MCU firmware         | Set by the risk assessment for the stop it triggers |
| Base aisle-speed ceiling             | SLS on the drive wheels, switched by the scanner's field set | IEC 61800-5-2; speed control under ISO 3691-4       | Set by ISO 3691-4 and the risk assessment           |
| Person at the rack end               | Scanner protective field that selects `STOP`                 | ISO 3691-4 person detection; ISO 13855 field sizing | PL d                                                |
| `STOP` on the base                   | Ramp-monitored SS1 (SS1-r), then parking brake               | IEC 61800-5-2; ISO 3691-4 braking control           | PL d for braking control; PL b for parking brake    |
| `HOLD`                               | SS2 into SOS                                                 | IEC 61800-5-2                                       | PL d on the arm; base set by the risk assessment    |
| `INHIBIT`                            | STO with SBC                                                 | IEC 61800-5-2; IEC 60204-1 Category 0               | PL d on the arm; base as for braking control        |
| Arm TCP, latch, and handover limits  | Safety-rated monitored speed in the arm's safety controller  | ISO 10218-1:2025                                    | PL d (Class II)                                     |
| Handover to the coworker's hand      | Speed and separation monitoring or power and force limiting  | ISO 10218-2:2025                                    | Set by the application risk assessment              |

: **The permission path above its certified floor**: Each response and speed channel of this chapter beside the safety-rated function that carries the certified claim on a production machine, the requirement that governs it, and the performance level that requirement sets for this machine. Only the first row has no certified counterpart; its checks are the performance layer. The second row is the one rated function on the MCU. {#tbl-12-certified-functions tbl-colwidths="[24,28,26,22]"}

The first row highlights a fundamental engineering reality: the online control barrier function quadratic program (CBF-QP), feasibility tests, and sensor evidence-age checks operate without formal safety ratings. Consequently, safety cases cannot cite these complex numerical filters as certified protective measures; instead, the enforcement record treats their correct execution as an operational premise. System architects face two choices when structuring this boundary. An engineering team can treat all MCU-level admission checks strictly as an unrated performance layer, relying entirely on the certified hardware floor to prevent harm. Alternatively, the team can certify the entire MCU firmware stack to functional safety standards (such as IEC 61508 or ISO 26262), subjecting matrix solvers and barrier algorithms to exhaustive formal methods, tool qualification, and deterministic execution bounds.

This book demonstrates a pragmatic, hybrid architecture. Only the supervisory watchdog in the second row is certified: when a command lease expires or the host heartbeat falls silent, it independently commands STO or SS1 at the drive level. Because this watchdog logic is minimal, it readily complies with rigorous safety software lifecycles. Meanwhile, the complex admission checks remain unrated, leaving the certified optical scanner and drive-integrated safety functions to handle primary hazard mitigation. This split architecture demands strict physical and temporal isolation between the rated watchdog and unrated solver routines to eliminate common-cause faults (@sec-placement-two-paths-one-die). The release criteria developed in @sec-release-safety-cases-claims formalize how these tiered claims are validated.

The robotic arm introduces collaborative operational modes beyond those required by the mobile base. **Speed and separation monitoring (SSM)**\index{Speed and separation monitoring} continuously modulates or halts arm velocity to maintain a protective clearance envelope around human workers, while **power and force limiting (PFL)**\index{Power and force limiting} caps transient and quasi-static contact forces during intentional physical collaboration. Standard ISO 10218-2:2025 incorporates the collaborative requirements previously defined in ISO/TS 15066 [@iso10218part2; @isots15066]. The 2025 standard formalizes SSM within section 5.14.5 and normative Annex L, and specifies PFL limits across anatomical regions in section 5.14.6 and informative Annex M [@hartmann2026evolution]. The protective separation distance is governed by:
$$S_p = S_h + S_r + S_s + C + Z_d + Z_r,$$
where $S_h = v_h (T_r + T_s)$ represents worker displacement during robot reaction latency $T_r$ and stopping duration $T_s$, $S_r = v_r T_r$ is robot displacement prior to brake onset, $S_s$ is the physical braking distance, $C$ is the penetration distance permitted by sensor resolution, and $Z_d$ and $Z_r$ denote positional uncertainties for the human and robot, respectively [@marvel2017implementing].

Evaluating this expression for the descending arm highlights the relative weight of human vs. robot motion. With an ISO 13855 human approach speed $v_h =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.v_h_str` [@iso13855], a vision-path latency $T_r =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.t_r_str`, a tool-center-point velocity $v_r =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.v_r_str`, and the gravity-biased joint deceleration from @sec-enforcement-exhausted-authority (which completes in $T_s =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.t_s_str` across $S_s =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.s_s_str`), the human displacement term is $S_h =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.s_h_str` and the robot reaction displacement is $S_r =$ `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.s_r_str`. Together, these preliminary dynamic components total `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.s_partial_str` before accounting for sensor intrusion margin $C$ and spatial uncertainties $Z_d$ and $Z_r$.

Crucially, human movement accounts for `{python} EnforcementCertifiedFunctions.share_h_str` of this cumulative margin. Just as in the walking-person stopping budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget, human velocity during the combined reaction and deceleration phases dominates the required clearance: against an approaching human, total stopping duration imposes a far heavier spatial tax than the robot's physical braking distance alone. Because standard vision pipelines lack functional safety ratings, a certified SSM implementation must utilize dedicated, safety-qualified sensors to measure separation and bound $T_r$.

The standards establish an essential distinction regarding obstacle velocity. Standard ISO 3691-4 specifies detection assuming a stationary person standing in the travel path [@tuv2021iso3691]; consequently, vehicle testing protocols evaluate protective envelopes against the static-obstacle formulation of @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope. If a worker continues walking toward the vehicle throughout the braking sequence, the relative closing velocity exceeds the standard's baseline assumptions. In contrast, SSM explicitly models dynamic human approach velocity ($v_h$), explaining why mobile base navigation requires an explicit aisle-crossing protocol whereas robotic manipulation requires an active separation or contact-limiting channel. For collaborative handoffs, the enforcement record adopts the standardized biomechanical model of the human hand, distinguishing between unconstrained (transient) and clamped (quasi-static) contact scenarios. While simplified models often approximate PFL as a single lumped elastic collision with a fixed force threshold, ISO 10218-2 specifies distinct permissible force and pressure ceilings across individual anatomical regions. A complete architectural map correlating each subsystem, governing regulatory standard, and validation artifact is synthesized in the release decision framework (@tbl-16-standards-map).

::: {#chk-enforcement-fallback-ladder-preemption .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing the physical fallback"}

Before selecting a defensive fallback strategy, verify your understanding of state-dependent stopping modes, safety functions, and timing reserves:

- [ ] **State-dependent stop**: Why can powered braking be safer than STO for a moving AMR, while drive torque inhibit may be appropriate after a separately verified restraint holds a stationary arm?
- [ ] **Independent functions**: What does STO inhibit, and which separate functions would remove bus power or apply a spring brake?
- [ ] **Timing and clearance**: Which measured detection, dispatch, drive, and brake delays belong in the stop reservation?
- [ ] **Lost viability**: What can a fallback still accomplish when the admissible torque set is empty?

:::
## Runtime Enforcement Failure Modes {#sec-enforcement-failure-modes}

A safety filter cannot protect a machine if the physical computer executing it fails, nor can a flawless solver prevent a collision if its internal kinematic model no longer matches reality. Mathematical runtime enforcement mechanisms—such as control barrier function quadratic programs (CBF-QPs), reachability monitors, and hardware interlocks—rely on operational assumptions that bridge abstract dynamic models and physical hardware. When these assumptions fail, the safety guarantee collapses. In physical AI systems, runtime enforcement failures consistently trace back to four concrete failure classes:

1. **Common-cause infrastructure failures**:
When the primary neural policy and the safety filter share power distribution rails, clock sources, reset lines, or thermal dissipation paths, a single electrical or physical fault can disable both systems simultaneously. For example, a sudden current spike from high-torque actuator acceleration can cause a brownout on an unregulated 12 V bus, resetting both the high-throughput neural accelerator and the real-time microcontroller tasked with monitoring it. Similarly, a shared board-level reset or clock drift can silence the safety monitor at the exact instant the primary policy issues an errant command.

2. **Timing overruns and execution jitter**:
Safety filters compute control adjustments within a discrete control loop. If a numerical quadratic program stalls, encounters ill-conditioned active sets, or suffers scheduling jitter on a non-deterministic operating system, the time spent solving directly consumes the robot's physical braking clearance. A safety monitor designed to intervene within 10 ms provides no protection if a solver timeout delays actuation by 50 ms while the vehicle travels at 5 m/s. During that 40 ms overrun, the robot penetrates the safe set boundary before the brakes engage. Enforcement therefore requires a deterministic worst-case execution time (WCET) and an autonomous fallback response—such as an independent hardware watchdog or safe-stop interlock—that activates the moment a deadline expires.

3. **Plant mismatch and unobservable state drift**:
An optimization solver evaluates safety against an internal dynamical model of the plant. If physical conditions change—such as rain reducing tire-road friction, an unexpected 20 kg payload shifting the center of mass, or motor winding heat degrading peak torque—the assumed control authority vanishes. The solver may calculate an admissible deceleration profile that is dynamically infeasible for the compromised hardware. Because embedded sensors cannot always observe these parameter shifts directly at runtime, systems must incorporate qualified uncertainty margins into safe set definitions or enforce strict operational design domain (ODD) boundaries that restrict vehicle speed when parameter confidence drops.

4. **Interconnect contention and transport delays**:
Even when the solver executes on time and the model is accurate, state reads and command writes must traverse physical communication buses, such as CAN, Ethernet, SPI, or PCIe. Shared bus traffic introduces queuing delays and arbitration jitter. If high-bandwidth sensor telemetry or unprioritized logging floods the interconnect, a critical joint position reading may arrive stale, or a safety-filtered motor command may sit in a transmission queue. In the worst case, bus priority inversion or dropped packets can cause the actuator to continue executing a previous high-velocity setpoint while the safety filter's brake command waits for bus access.

These failure classes impose distinct architectural requirements that cannot be satisfied simply by selecting an automotive microcontroller or executing a barrier function algorithm. Instead, they demand rigorous engineering evidence across four specific obligations:

- **Placement obligations**: Mitigating common-cause failures and communication contention requires physical and architectural isolation. Designers must isolate safety monitors onto independent hardware domains with separate power regulation, isolated clock trees, and dedicated, deterministic communication links. We analyze and validate these hardware placement strategies under competing synthetic workloads in @sec-placement.
- **Real-time execution guarantees**: Mitigating timing overruns requires strictly bounded execution cycles. Every safety filter must run within a hard real-time envelope with verified worst-case completion bounds. If a solver overruns its deadline, the architecture must transition unconditionally to a fail-safe state through a surviving hardware mechanism that operates independently of the primary compute pipeline.
- **Robust uncertainty calibration**: Mitigating plant mismatch requires parameter margins that account for worst-case degradation rather than nominal laboratory conditions. When operating outside tightly controlled environments, safe set boundaries must contract to compensate for unmodeled physical variations.
- **Enforcement provenance and logging**: An autonomous system must continuously record runtime enforcement evidence. The telemetry system must capture not only the approved actuator commands, but also the solver's execution latency, active constraints, slack variables, and sensor timestamps. Retaining this diagnostic trail alongside every permitted command ensures that post-incident analysis can distinguish between policy errors, physical plant anomalies, and hardware infrastructure faults.
## The Enforcement Record {#sec-enforcement-telemetry}

When a warehouse mobile manipulator halts at a rack end because runtime safety logic rejected a motion proposal, forensic analysis requires unambiguous provenance: which threshold failed, which physical detector measured the violation, and which fallback rung took control of the actuators? The **enforcement record**\index{Enforcement record} represents the tenth entry in the system record chain, marking the point where offline characterization converges with online execution. It formalizes runtime safety across three cooperating artifacts:

1. **The Enforcement Contract:** The signed, immutable specification compiled into microcontroller firmware that fixes qualified tracking bounds $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, barrier coefficients, timer deadlines, and fallback routing tables before deployment.
2. **The Admitted Command:** The record's per-tick output\index{Admitted command!per-tick output}. On each millisecond control cycle, the microcontroller gatekeeper generates an admitted command for transmission across the causal boundary. This payload contains the admitted or projected control $\mathbf{u}^*$, the verified barrier margin $h(\mathbf{x})$, tracking error validation $e(t) \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$, and the remaining hardware lease. The gatekeeper forwards only the bare setpoint and protective envelope to the motor drives, committing the complete supervisory state to the audit ledger.
3. **The Enforcement Audit Ledger:** The high-rate streaming forensic log that captures per-tick proposal evaluations, intervention vectors $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^* - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}$, quadratic programming (QP) solve latencies, and veto events in non-volatile storage.

Together, these artifacts render safety decisions fully auditable without burdening the actuator bus. The contract predefines the admissible operating envelope, the admitted command tags the immediate actuator setpoint, and the audit ledger preserves the causal chain of evidence. Real-time enforcement depends entirely on the protected command path, deterministic loop timing, and verified physical braking capabilities.

### The admitted command schema {#sec-enforcement-admitted-command-schema}

At each control cycle, the gatekeeper produces an admitted command that establishes runtime authority at the drive interface (@tbl-12-admitted-command-schema). Its fields explicitly bind the actuator setpoint to its parent trajectory, verified safety margins, and active fallback state. Because this record captures an evaluation evaluated under assumed physical conditions, runtime containment still relies on matching those assumptions to physical reality.

| Field Name                 | Type & Units            | Physical System Invariant & Validation Rule                                                                                                | Mobile Manipulator Parameter / Value                                                                                           |
|:---------------------------|:------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `token_sequence_id`        | `uint64_t` (counter)    | Monotonically increasing admitted-command ID on MCU clock                                                                                  | Increments every `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` tick                                                              |
| `timestamp_mcu_ns`         | `uint64_t` (ns)         | Absolute MCU monotonic timestamp of admission                                                                                              | Latch instant at causal boundary                                                                                               |
| `parent_trajectory_digest` | `uint8_t[32]` (SHA-256) | Cryptographic link to the admitted trajectory record and chunk lease                                                                       | SHA-256 of active trajectory record                                                                                            |
| `admitted_control_vector`  | `float32[N_act]` (N·m)  | Filtered torque $\mathbf{u}^*$ that the staged setpoint and torque limit realize; nominal if safe, projected if near boundary              | Per-axis qualified torque envelope; `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit_str` only for the characterized arm axis   |
| `intervention_vector`      | `float32[N_act]` (N·m)  | Intervention delta $\Delta \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^* - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}$; zero when the admitted command equals the nominal command | Nonzero only during CBF-QP projection                                                                                          |
| `barrier_margin`           | `float32` (normalized)  | Dimensionless $h(\mathbf{x})/h_{\mathrm{scale}}$ with positive scale and barrier identity bound in the contract                            | Must satisfy $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$                                                                                             |
| `tracking_error`           | `float32` (m)           | Instantaneous tracking error norm $e(t) = \lVert \mathbf{x}_{\text{meas}} - \mathbf{r}_{\text{cmd}} \rVert$                                | Base position error: $e(t) \le$ `{python} EnforcementTrackingBound.eps_track_str`; arm channels use their own qualified bounds |
| `active_fallback_rung`     | `uint8_t` (enum)        | Active execution state: `PROJECT`, `HOLD`, `STOP`, `INHIBIT`                                                                               | `0x01` (`PROJECT`) during nominal tracking                                                                                     |
| `lease_remaining_ns`       | `uint32_t` (ns)         | Remaining validity duration of current chunk lease                                                                                         | Trips `STOP` / `HOLD` upon reaching zero                                                                                       |
| `crc32_token`              | `uint32_t` (checksum)   | CRC-32 over the ledger entry, for audit integrity                                                                                          | Ledger reader rejects a corrupt entry; the drive-facing setpoint carries its own safety-layer CRC                              |

: **Admitted command schema**: The per-tick output of the enforcement record, the tenth record in the record chain. Formed on every `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` tick by the microcontroller and written to the audit ledger, identifying the selected command, checked assumptions, and state-matched response. The drives receive only the setpoint, torque limit, and active rung inside a black-channel safety message; drive hardware containment relies on the local safety watchdog rather than the record itself. {#tbl-12-admitted-command-schema tbl-colwidths="[22,18,34,26]"}

Constructing the enforcement record requires synthesizing four upstream records spanning both evidence strands. The offline strand establishes physical plant capabilities and empirical policy competence, while the runtime strand tracks live execution state:

- The trajectory record of @sec-planning-trajectory-contract supplies the admitted reference and its precomputed, dynamically feasible stop suffix.
- The evaluation record of @sec-evaluation-logs provides runtime monitor specifications and the empirical coverage-gap catalog, defining the active supervisory channels.
- The policy manifest of @sec-training-policy-manifest defines the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD), restricting the enforcer's validity region to well-sampled operating regimes.
- The limit records of @sec-body-measuring-limits establish empirical braking rates, actuator onset delays, and torque envelopes alongside their operating preconditions.

To these upstream parameters, the enforcement record contributes the formal guarantees of the gatekeeping pipeline: the qualified tracking bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, stopping metrics ($t_{\text{stop}}, d_{\text{stop}}$, which bound the duration and displacement required to arrest plant momentum), Control Barrier Function\index{Control barrier function} coefficients, the discrete execution period, per-check thresholds mapped to fallback-ladder rungs, and the dynamic validity boundary.

The `parent_trajectory_digest` binds each admitted command to its originating trajectory and active chunk lease, providing forensic traceability back to the planner's proposal. While cryptographic digests verify data integrity, preventing replay attacks and confirming sender authenticity require complementary sequence counters and monotonic freshness checks within the protected drive interface. Similarly, the `lease_remaining_ns` field conveys remaining execution authority, but this parameter guarantees safety only when the drive firmware actively enforces lease expiration by triggering a deterministic physical fallback. Streaming these fields—alongside nominal proposals, intervention deltas, barrier margins, tracking errors, and solver latencies—to the audit ledger gives engineers the causal evidence needed to reconstruct anomalous behaviors within the temporal resolution of the sensor pipeline.

This division of responsibilities dictates an architectural split at the fieldbus boundary. Motor drives have no operational need for trajectory digests or barrier margins; they require immediate setpoints, current limits, and active fallback commands delivered with fail-safe transport guarantees. Industrial systems handle this through established safety bus architectures. For example, Safety over EtherCAT (FSoE) implements the **black-channel principle**\index{Black-channel principle!drive interface}, treating the underlying communication bus as inherently untrusted [@iec61784-3-2021]. FSoE encapsulates drive commands within an authenticated safety container featuring dedicated cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs), unique connection identifiers, strict sequence counters, and independent watchdog timers. When a communication watchdog expires, the drive autonomously engages its safe stop state without waiting for microcontroller intervention. Meanwhile, the rich diagnostic context—including digests, barrier margins, intervention vectors, and solver runtimes—streams directly to the forensic audit ledger. Designing an ad hoc transport security scheme for drive control merely replicates established functional-safety standards while forfeiting their formal certification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ High-rate enforcer refusal events populate the forensic evidence logs analyzed in @sec-intervention-authority-log.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-record-machine
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE ENFORCEMENT RECORD ON THE MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the record list, the routing paragraph, and the approach-ceiling
# │          paragraph of @sec-enforcement-telemetry.
# │ Goal:    fill the record's fields with the base's and the arm's own values.
# │ Show:    tracking bound; resident stop at the aisle speed and drive limit;
# │          both base configurations; the latch approach and its projection;
# │          the free-space TCP limit and the handover ceiling under accept_item.
# │ How:     calc_scurve_stop_time / _distance on RM/AISLE with the jerk bound
# │          and inspected-floor peak from EnforcementStoppingBudget;
# │          calc_contact_yield_deadline for the door; the handover ceilings
# │          from EnforcementContactForce (@sec-enforcement-intentional-contact).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_stop_distance, calc_scurve_stop_time, calc_contact_yield_deadline
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementRecordMachine:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    eps_track = AISLE.eps_track  # category: illustrative
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    mu_min = EnforcementStoppingBudget.mu_min  # category: derived (a_brake / g)
    mu_inspected = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative
    a_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.a_inspected  # category: derived (mu_inspected_floor * g)
    v_inspected = EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_inspected  # category: derived
    v_restricted = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: chosen (restricted-mode aisle speed, below the inspected-floor ceiling)
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (target-ODD approach)
    k_latch = AISLE.k_latch  # category: illustrative
    f_latch_limit = AISLE.f_latch_limit  # category: illustrative
    t_contact = AISLE.t_contact_response  # category: illustrative (contact loop)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen (free-space TCP limit)
    v_handover = AISLE.v_handover  # category: chosen (handover approach under accept_item)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    j_brake = EnforcementStoppingBudget.j_brake  # category: derived (reference polynomial's peak jerk)
    t_stop_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    d_stop_aisle = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    t_stop_drive = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_drive, a_brake, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    d_stop_drive = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_drive, a_brake, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    t_stop_restricted = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_restricted, a_inspected, j_brake).to(millisecond)
    d_stop_restricted = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_restricted, a_inspected, j_brake).to(millimeter)
    t_yield_high = calc_contact_yield_deadline(f_latch_limit, k_latch, v_latch_high).to(millisecond)
    v_handover_ceiling = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling  # derived in calc-enforcement-contact-force
    v_handover_ceiling_clamped = EnforcementContactForce.v_ceiling_clamped  # derived in calc-enforcement-contact-force

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_track.to(millimeter).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "The base's tracking bound is 40 mm.")
    check(abs(t_stop_aisle.magnitude - 931.25) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s takes 931.25 ms.")
    check(abs(d_stop_aisle.magnitude - 605.3125) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.3 m/s covers 605.31 mm.")
    check(abs(t_stop_drive.magnitude - 1031.25) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.5 m/s takes 1031.25 ms.")
    check(abs(d_stop_drive.magnitude - 773.4375) < 1e-6, "The S-curve stop from 1.5 m/s covers 773.44 mm.")
```
